هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةُ فِيهَا قَوْلَانِ عِنْدَ الْإِطْلَاقِ مَعْرُوفَانِ لِلْفُقَهَاءِ فِي مَذْهَبِ الْإِمَامِ أَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِ؛ وَلَكِنَّ الْأَقْوَى أَنَّهَا لِتَرْتِيبِ الْأَفْرَادِ عَلَى الْأَفْرَادِ وَأَنَّ وَلَدَ الْوَلَدِ يَقُومُ مَقَامَ أَبِيهِ لَوْ كَانَ الِابْنُ مَوْجُودًا مُسْتَحِقًّا قَدْ عَاشَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِ الْجَدِّ وَاسْتَحَقَّ أَوْ عَاشَ وَلَمْ يَسْتَحِقَّ لِمَانِعِ فِيهِ أَوْ لِعَدَمِ قَبُولِهِ لِلْوَقْفِ أَوْ لِغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ أَوْ لَمْ يَعِشْ بَلْ مَاتَ فِي حَيَاةِ الْجَدِّ. وَيَكُونُ عَلَى هَذَا التَّقْدِيرِ مُقَابَلَةُ الْجَمْعِ بِالْجَمْعِ؛ وَهِيَ تَقْتَضِي تَوْزِيعَ الْأَفْرَادِ عَلَى الْأَفْرَادِ كَمَا فِي قَوْلِهِ 
{وَلَكُمْ نِصْفُ مَا تَرَكَ أَزْوَاجُكُمْ}
 أَيْ لِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ نِصْفُ مَا تَرَكَتْ زَوْجَتُهُ؛
 وَقَوْلُهُ:
 
{حُرِّمَتْ عَلَيْكُمْ أُمَّهَاتُكُمْ}
 أَيْ حُرِّمَ عَلَى كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ أُمُّهُ وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ.
 كَذَلِكَ قَوْلُهُ:
 عَلَى أَوْلَادِهِمْ؛
 ثُمَّ عَلَى أَوْلَادِ أَوْلَادِهِمْ أَيْ:
 عَلَى كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ بَعْدَ مَوْتِ أَبِيهِ. وَأَمَّا فِي هَذِهِ فَقَدْ صَرَّحَ الْوَاقِفُ بِأَنَّهُ مَنْ مَاتَ عَنْ وَلَدٍ انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهُ إلَى وَلَدِهِ؛ وَهَذَا صَرِيحٌ فِي أَنَّهُ لِتَرْتِيبِ الْأَفْرَادِ عَلَى الْأَفْرَادِ؛ فَلَمْ يَبْقَ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ نِزَاعٌ. وَإِنَّمَا الشُّبْهَةُ فِي أَنَّ الْوَلَدَ إذَا مَاتَ فِي حَيَاةِ أَبِيهِ وَلَهُ وَلَدٌ؛
 ثُمَّ مَاتَ الْأَبُ عَنْ وَلَدٍ آخَرَ وَعَنْ وَلَدِ الْوَلَدِ الْأَوَّلِ:
 هَلْ يَشْتَرِكَانِ؟ أَوْ يَنْفَرِدُ بِهِ الْأَوَّلُ؟
translated_text:
Do they, then, share her portion, or is the son alone entitled to it, to the exclusion of the son’s daughter?

The aforementioned son then died leaving a son. Is he alone entitled to what his father had been receiving, to the exclusion of the son’s daughter? Does the founder’s aforementioned stipulation require one entire generation to succeed another, or individuals to succeed their respective predecessors?

He replied:

Where the wording is unqualified, there are two well-known views on this question among the jurists of Imam Ahmad’s school and other schools. The stronger view, however, is that it establishes individual succession: a grandchild takes the place his father would have occupied had he been alive and entitled. This applies whether the son survived the grandfather and became entitled; survived but did not become entitled because of an impediment affecting him, because he did not accept the endowment, or for some other reason; or did not survive the grandfather, but died during his lifetime.

On this interpretation, one plural expression is set against another, which requires each individual in one group to correspond to the respective individual in the other. Thus, Allah says:

“You shall have half of what your wives leave.”

That is, each man receives half of what his own wife leaves. Likewise, His words:

“You are forbidden to marry your mothers.”

That is, each man is forbidden to marry his own mother. Other expressions follow the same pattern.

Similarly, the founder’s words, “for their children, then for their children’s children,” mean that each succeeds after his own father’s death. In the present case, moreover, the founder explicitly stipulated that, when someone dies leaving a child, his share passes to his child. This expressly establishes individual succession, leaving no room for disagreement on this point in the present case.

The only uncertainty concerns a child who dies during his father’s lifetime, leaving a child of his own. The father then dies leaving another child and the child of his first child: do these two share, or is the former alone entitled to the portion?

translated_text:
The stronger view in this case is that the two share. For if the intention is that each child becomes entitled after his father’s death—whether his paternal uncle is alive or dead—then such wording makes entitlement conditional upon the father’s lack of entitlement. This is comparable to what the jurists say regarding the order of agnatic heirs: the son, then his son, then the father, then his father, then the paternal uncle, then the paternal uncle’s sons, and so forth.

The only condition for the second rank is that the first should have no entitlement. Whenever members of the second rank exist and those of the first have no entitlement, the second becomes entitled, whether or not the first had previously been entitled. Entitlement at the second rank does not require prior entitlement at the first. This is because the second generation receives its entitlement to the endowment from the founder, not from that second generation itself. It is not like property inherited by a son and then passed on to his son. Rather, it resembles the bond of manumission, by virtue of which one inherits: if the emancipator’s son dies during the emancipator’s lifetime, his son’s son inherits the entitlement arising from that bond.

Those who err in cases of this kind do so because they suppose that the second generation receives its entitlement from the preceding one, so that if the first was not entitled to anything, neither is the second. They therefore suppose that if a father dies before becoming entitled, his son has no entitlement. This is not so; rather, they receive their entitlement from the founder.

This holds even if the first generation is excluded by an impediment. For example, the founder may stipulate that the beneficiaries must be poor, scholars, upright people, or meet some other condition. If the father does not meet the stipulated condition but his son does, the son becomes entitled even though his father did not. Likewise, if he dies

The same applies to every order of priority in child custody, guardianship over marriage and property, inheritance through agnatic kinship or the bond of manumission, and all other matters in which those entitled are arranged in successive ranks and degrees: the principle is as explained above.

This is what founders of endowments intend when asked about their meaning. Those who state their intention explicitly explain that the grandchild is to receive what the founder’s child would have received had he been alive. This is especially so because people feel compassion for someone whose father has died and who has inherited nothing; a grandfather may even make a bequest to his grandchild. It is well known that this grandchild and the other son’s child stand in the same relationship to the grandfather. How, then, could he deprive his orphaned grandchild while giving to his grandchild who is not an orphan? No reasonable person would intend this.

If we do not hold that they share, the endowment remains confined to this son and his offspring, excluding the descendants of the son who died during his father’s lifetime. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A woman established an endowment to support her tomb after her death. She allocated a specified amount to Quran reciters, with any surplus going to the poor or charitable causes. She has a relative—her maternal uncle—who has become impoverished and needy and is no longer in service. The administrator has not provided him with enough to sustain him. Must the administrator be compelled to provide for this relative’s subsistence and meet his needs in preference to others?

He answered:

If the woman who established the endowment has a needy relative, such as a maternal uncle or the like, he has a greater claim than an unrelated poor person whose need is equal to his, and he should be given priority. If the endowment has sufficient resources to meet his needs, they should be met from it.

translated_text:
the ruler. The ruler has established an office for each of these categories to safeguard its endowments and distribute their proceeds to their designated purposes. The administrator considers it appropriate to appoint an auditor specifically for these transactions—meaning all the endowments—to examine their accounts, review the actions of the administrators and managing officials, verify the sums spent and remaining for which they must account, and maintain records of this. This would safeguard the endowments’ funds as they pass through different hands and managing officials are replaced. His oversight evidently encourages some officials to exercise care, producing a benefit. May the ruler do this if he considers it beneficial, or not?

If he now proceeds with this because he considers it beneficial, appoints the aforementioned auditor, and assigns him a small fixed stipend charged to each of these endowments—far below the regular income of any of their managing officials—because of the benefit he sees in it, is that permissible? Is the aforementioned auditor entitled to receive his stipulated remuneration if he performs his duties?

If his duty is to obtain each year’s accounts in accordance with the procedures followed by the scribes, and he finds accounts submitted for several years or more, which he then processes in fulfilment of his duties, is he entitled to remuneration for the period whose accounts he obtained and examined in the performance of those duties?

He answered:

Yes. The ruler may establish an office to audit the accounts of endowed funds when this serves a beneficial purpose, just as he may establish offices to audit state revenues, such as fay’ revenues and the like. He may also assign the auditor remuneration for his work commensurate with what someone in his position deserves:

from each fund he administers, in proportion to the size of that fund. Auditing accounts and keeping accurate records of receipts and expenditure are duties with an established basis in the words of the Most High:

“and those employed to administer it”

And in an authentic hadith:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, appointed a man to collect zakat, and when he returned, he examined his accounts.”

This establishes a basis for auditing officials working in different places. The central auditor acts as the ruler’s deputy in examining their accounts. Where funds are numerous and their officials must be audited, a central office is indispensable. Thus, when revenues increased during the time of the Commander of the Faithful, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, he established administrative offices: the land-tax office, which was the office for personnel employed on stipends, and placed ʿUthmān ibn Hunayf in charge of it; and the expenditure office, which handled disbursements to fighting men and their descendants and resembled the office of al-habs and al-thubūtāt and similar offices in our own time. He placed Zayd ibn Thābit in charge of it.

Likewise, those in authority—the ruler, the judge, and others like them—must administer endowed funds according to valid conditions consistent with the Book of Allah, and appoint officials for work to which the endowment administrator has appointed none. In the terminology of Islamic law, an official includes the person called an administrator, as well as others charged with collecting money from those who owe it and disbursing and delivering it to those entitled to it, in accordance with His words:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to whom they are due.”

The appointment of a central auditor to oversee officials working in different places depends on need and benefit. It may be obligatory if the proper collection and disbursement of funds cannot be achieved without it, for that without which

The same applies to the ruler’s appointment of a judge: he must appoint one when need and public benefit require it, if rights cannot otherwise reach those entitled to them, or obligations cannot be fulfilled and prohibited acts avoided. The ruler may dispense with a judge if he can adjudicate personally.

In places distant from him, he appointed someone to undertake these duties. When the population under Muslim rule increased during the time of Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, and the other caliphs, they appointed judges and established administrative offices in their garrison cities and elsewhere. Thus, ʿUmar appointed Zayd ibn Thābit as his deputy in Medina to oversee judicial affairs and the administrative office.

In Kufa, he appointed ʿAmmār ibn Yāsir to lead the prayers and command the army—combining the roles of the ruler’s deputy and the preacher—for the established sunnah was that the military commander would lead the people in prayer. He appointed ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿūd to oversee judicial affairs and the public treasury, and ʿUthmān ibn Hunayf to oversee the land-tax office.

When the central auditor performs his assigned duties, he is entitled to the stipend allocated to him and any remuneration he was lawfully permitted to stipulate. If he performs this work but is not paid his remuneration, he may seek payment for the particular work, for whatever becomes due through a transaction must be paid.

He was asked:

A man leased plots of endowed land and planted trees on them, which bore fruit. Once the lease term had elapsed, the trustees of the endowment wished to uproot the trees. Are they entitled to do so, or are they entitled to the fair rental value? Will the ruler be rewarded for assisting him?

He replied:

Those responsible for the land are not entitled to uproot the trees. Rather, they may demand the fair rental value, acquire the trees at their assessed value, or compensate for their loss in value if they are uprooted. As long as the trees remain, their owner must pay the fair rental value. The ruler must prevent the wrongdoer from committing injustice. Allah knows best.

He was also asked—may Allah have mercy on him:

A man has served for several years as the imam and preacher of a mosque and as the administrator of its endowment, by decree of the ruler. He is entitled to remuneration by virtue of his lawful appointment. May the trustees of another endowment take control of this endowment or administer it without this administrator, spend the mosque’s funds on purposes other than those designated for them, or withhold the remuneration allocated to him for these duties? Even supposing that this endowment had been registered with their administrative office for some time, and then

the ruler removed it from their administration and entrusted it to the imam and preacher, are they entitled, in these circumstances, to administer it and prevent him from doing so while his appointment remains in force? If someone unlawfully administers it and diverts some of its funds to someone else, while the imam is in need and the mosque’s services are being maintained, and persists in doing so under these circumstances, does this impugn his religious commitment and uprightness or not?

He replied:

No administrator other than the one entrusted with this endowment may take control of it or administer it without his permission—neither the trustees of another endowment nor anyone else—whether or not they previously administered it. Nor may they, in the circumstances described, spend the mosque’s funds on purposes other than those for which they were endowed. Rather, the imam and others must be paid their entitlements in full. Their entitlements must not be reduced in order to divert the resulting surplus to another endowment, for there is no disagreement that this is impermissible.

The scholars differed only over whether surplus funds may be transferred. Even those who permitted this did not allow anyone other than the appointed administrator to act independently in doing so. Whoever persists in disbursing funds to someone not entitled to them while withholding them from the rightful recipient thereby impugns his religious commitment and uprightness.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A person established an endowment for poor Muslims. May its administrator, in these circumstances, distribute all its income to three people or not? If he may distribute it to three people, and the founder has a poor relative whose poverty and entitlement to receive from this endowment have been established, may that relative receive a share in place of one of the three beneficiaries unrelated to the founder?

If he may receive a share, should he be given priority over the two unrelated beneficiaries? If he should be given priority, may the administrator, in these circumstances, give the founder’s relative enough from the endowment to meet his needs? If that is permissible, is doing so preferable and better than giving him less than he needs and distributing the difference to an unrelated person in these circumstances?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. The administrator of an endowment must exercise his best judgment in distributing its proceeds, giving priority to those most entitled, in descending order. If a benefit recognized by Islamic law requires distributing it to three people—for example, because any less would not suffice for them—he should not include other poor people alongside them. If it suffices for them and for other poor people, he should include those others and treat them equally in distributing the income it yields. They have a stronger claim than he does when claims compete, and in similar circumstances. And the relatives of

If any of its property is surplus to the needs of the institution under his charge, may he devote it to another important purpose and to necessary repairs that might preserve it, given the frequent encroachments upon it, or not?

He replied:

The underlying principle here is that whatever Allah has required of obedience to Him and fear of Him is conditional upon ability. As He, Most High, says:

“So fear Allah as much as you are able.”

And as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“When I command you to do something, do as much of it as you can.”

Accordingly, when benefits and harms conflict, Islamic law requires securing the greater of two benefits by forgoing the lesser, and tolerating the lesser of two harms to avert the greater. Thus, if serious harm to these endowed funds and their lawful disbursement can only be prevented through what has been mentioned—tolerating a lesser harm—then that is what Islamic law requires. If this becomes this man’s individual duty, he may not abandon it unless undertaking it involves harm or conflicts with a more pressing obligation.

By the consensus of the Muslims, he may receive remuneration for his work in administering them when he is in need. Indeed, some have permitted this even when he is well-off, just as Allah, Most High, has permitted those employed to administer zakat to receive payment even when they have no need of it.

If an endowed property falls into ruin and ceases to provide any benefit, it is to be sold and its price spent on a comparable property, or it may be transferred to a comparable one. Likewise, if any of the places supported by an endowment fall into ruin

—such as a mosque or the like—to the point that restoration is impossible, the income from the endowment supporting it is to be directed elsewhere. “Are these relatives among the ashrāf or not? May they receive anything from the endowment or not?”

He replied:

The same applies when someone establishes an endowment for the “ashrāf,” since customary usage includes under this designation only those whose descent from the household of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is genuine. If, however, someone establishes an endowment for the descendants or relatives of a particular person, or the like, and nothing in its terms indicates that it is intended for the Prophet’s household, and the endowed property belongs to the founder and may validly be endowed for that particular person’s descendants, then the descendants of Hāshim are not included in this endowment.

He was also asked—may Allah sanctify his soul—about a man who holds a mosque appointment under written authorizations to revive a practice prescribed by Islamic law, following the previous holder’s relinquishment of the appointment through a written instrument validated by the judges. The son of the man who originally held the appointment then challenged its present holder and demanded to share it with him. He had no basis in Islamic law other than the fact that his father had held it. May the present holder be compelled to share the appointment without his consent?

translated_text:
He replied:

Praise be to Allah. In these circumstances, it is not permissible to compel the imam of a mosque to share his appointment, to appoint the two men jointly, or to dismiss him merely on the grounds mentioned—that the other man’s father was the imam. Mosque appointments must be given to those most entitled to them under Islamic law: those most proficient in reciting the Book of Allah, most knowledgeable about the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and having precedence in righteous deeds—for example, by having emigrated earlier or being older. How much more so when the person most entitled to the appointment already holds it! The scholars agree that he may not be dismissed. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

About a school endowed for jurists and students of jurisprudence of a specified group, to provide them with accommodation and a place to pursue their studies: is accommodation restricted to those receiving stipends? Is it permissible to evict a resident who belongs to the category for which the endowment was established?

He replied:

Accommodation and receipt of a stipend are not restricted to a single individual. It is permissible to reside there without receiving a stipend from the funds, just as it is permissible to receive a stipend without residing there. No member of either category may be deprived of his entitlement without a valid reason under Islamic law—provided the resident is engaged in study—whether or not he attends the lesson.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy upon him—was asked:

About a man who transferred to another person ownership of property standing on land endowed for the benefit of the aforementioned person and others during his lifetime, and, after his death, for his children and any further children Allah might grant him, male and female, in equal shares, on the following conditions:

If any of them dies leaving a child, his share of the endowment shall pass to his child, or his grandchild or more remote descendants, whether one or more, male or female, descended through sons or daughters. Males and females shall receive equal shares. If he dies leaving no child, grandchild or more remote descendant, his share shall pass to those of the same degree of kinship, in addition to their entitlement to the income of this endowment. If he has neither a brother nor a sister, nor anyone of the same degree of kinship, his share shall pass to his nearest relatives, in order of proximity, through both male and female lines. The higher generation shall exclude the lower generation, with descendants through male and female lines treated equally, until they have all died out.

If no one remains whose lineage goes back to the beneficiary, whether through the father or through the daughter, the income of the endowment shall be allocated to the poor and needy in the protected frontier port of Damietta, those arriving there and those who frequent it. The administrator shall distribute it as he sees fit. Thereafter, it shall be allocated to Muslim captives.

original_text:
فَمِنْ أَهْلِ الْوَقْفِ الْأَوَّلِ أَحَدُ الْبَنَاتِ تُوُفِّيَتْ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهَا وَلَدٌ أَخَذَ إخْوَتُهَا نَصِيبُهَا؛ ثُمَّ مَاتَتْ الْبِنْتُ الثَّانِيَةُ وَلَهَا ابْنَتَانِ أَخَذَتَا نَصِيبَهَا؛ ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ مَاتَتْ الْبِنْتُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهَا وَلَدٌ أَخَذَتْ أُخْتُهَا نَصِيبَهَا ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ مَاتَتْ الْأُخْتُ الرَّابِعَةُ فَأَخَذُوا لَهَا الثُّلُثَيْنِ. فَهَلْ يَصِحُّ لِأَوْلَادِ خَالَتِهِ نَصِيبٌ مَعَهُ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، الْبِنْتُ الْأُولَى انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهَا إلَى إخْوَتِهَا الثَّلَاثَةِ؛ كَمَا شَرَطَهُ الْوَاقِفُ؛ لَا يُشَارِكُ أَوْلَادُ هَذِهِ لِأَوْلَادِ هَذِهِ فِي النَّصِيبِ الْأَصْلِيِّ الَّذِي كَانَ لِأُمِّهَا. وَأَمَّا النَّصِيبُ الْعَائِدُ - وَهُوَ الَّذِي كَانَ لِلثَّالِثَةِ وَانْتَقَلَ إلَى الرَّابِعَةِ - فَهَذَا يَشْتَرِكُ فِيهِ أَوْلَادُ هَذِهِ وَأَوْلَادُ هَذِهِ؛ كَمَا يَشْتَرِكُ فِيهِ أُمُّهُمَا هَذَا أَظْهَرُ الْقَوْلَيْنِ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ.

 لِأَنَّ الْوَاقِفَ قَالَ:
 وَإِنْ تُوُفِّيَ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ وَلَدٌ وَلَا وَلَدُ وَلَدٍ وَلَا أَسْفَلَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ كَانَ نَصِيبُهُ مَصْرُوفًا إلَى مَنْ فِي دَرَجَتِهِ مُضَافٌ إلَى مَا يَسْتَحِقُّهُ مِنْ رِيعِ الْوَقْفِ.

 فَالْمُضَافُ كَالْمُضَافِ إلَيْهِ فَإِذَا كَانَ هَذَا يَنْتَقِلُ إلَى أَوْلَادِهِ فَكَذَلِكَ الْآخَرُ: لِأَنَّ قَوْلَ الْوَاقِفِ: مَنْ مَاتَ مِنْهُمْ وَتَرَكَ وَلَدًا كَانَ نَصِيبُهُ مِنْ الْوَقْفِ إلَى وَلَدِهِ يَتَنَاوَلُ الْأَصْلِيَّ وَالْعَائِدَ. وَالْأَظْهَرُ هُوَ الْقَوْلُ الْأَوَّلُ؛
 فَإِنَّ قَوْلَهُ:
 كَانَ نَصِيبُهُ. يَتَنَاوَلُ النَّصِيبَ
translated_text:
One of the daughters among the beneficiaries of the original endowment died without leaving any children, and her siblings received her share. Then the second daughter died, leaving two daughters, who received her share. After that, the third daughter died without leaving any children, and her sister received her share. Then the fourth sister died, and they took the two-thirds share on her behalf. Are his maternal aunt’s children entitled to a share alongside him, or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. The first daughter’s share passed to her three siblings, as stipulated by the founder of the endowment. The children of one sister do not share with the children of the other in the original share that belonged to the mother of those other children. As for the reallocated share—the share that belonged to the third sister and passed to the fourth—the children of both sisters share in it, just as their mother shares in it. This is the stronger of the two opinions on this question.

Another opinion holds that everything the fourth sister received—her own share and the third sister’s share—passes exclusively to her children, because the founder stipulated:

“If he dies leaving no child, grandchild or more remote descendant, his share shall pass to those of the same degree of kinship, in addition to their entitlement to the income of the endowment.”

Those who hold this opinion argue that the added share has the same status as the share to which it is added. Since the latter passes to his children, so does the former, because the founder’s stipulation, “If any of them dies leaving a child, his share of the endowment shall pass to his child,” encompasses both the original and the reallocated shares.

The first opinion, however, is stronger, for his words, “his share shall be,” encompass the share

The founder’s wording and customary usage evidently indicate that he treated members of the same generation equally with regard to the share of someone who had a child. The other beneficiary received it because he belonged to that same generation, and his children belong to the same generation as the children of the first deceased. Just as the two deceased beneficiaries would have shared in this reallocated share had they both been alive, so their children share in it after them, for both sets of children bear the same relationship to its original holder. This is what people intend by such stipulations, as their customary usage and practice attest.

The aim is to administer the endowment according to the stipulations intended by its founder. Hence the jurists said: “His provisions are like the texts of the Lawgiver”—meaning in how they are understood and what they signify. Their intended meaning may thus be understood in various ways, just as the Lawgiver’s intent is understood. Anyone who examines the circumstances of endowment founders knows that this is what they intend, for it is more consistent with justice. The grandchildren all bear the same relationship to the founder, so he has no purpose in giving one beneficiary’s son two or three shares merely because his father died later, while the others receive only one share. translated_text:
Shaykh al-Islām Ahmad ibn Taymiyyah—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A founder established an endowment for his children, then his children’s children, then his children’s children’s children, and his descendants and posterity, in perpetuity for as long as they continue to have descendants, stipulating:

“If any of them dies leaving neither a child nor a grandchild, nor descendants nor posterity, whatever he had been receiving from this endowment shall pass to those of his degree of kinship and generation.”

If one of these beneficiaries dies leaving a child, a grandchild, descendants or posterity, to whom does his share belong? Does it belong to his child, or to those of his degree of kinship, such as his brothers, paternal cousins and the like?

He replied:

His share passes to his child, not to his brothers or paternal cousins, for several reasons, three of which we shall mention.

The first is that the founder’s statement, “For his children, then his children’s children,” is restricted by the qualification that follows it, namely:

“On condition that, if any of them dies leaving no child, his share shall pass to those of his generation.”

Whenever a statement is joined to something that restricts it, that restriction must be taken into account, rather than treating the opening words as unrestricted.

To explain the first premise: this clause—“On condition that, if any of them dies”—functions syntactically as a circumstantial clause in the accusative position. A circumstantial clause conveys a qualifying description, and a qualifying description restricts what it describes.

And, if you wish, you may say: because it is a prepositional phrase attached to the verb, and a prepositional phrase functions as an object in negation, thereby restricting the verb.

Or, if you wish, you may say: because it is a statement that does not stand independently and must therefore be joined to what precedes it.

Or, if you wish, you may say: because the speaker did not stop at the initial statement, but joined further words to it, and that continuation restricts it. All these principles are self-evident in every language.

To explain the second premise: whenever a statement is joined to a qualifying description, a condition, or any other wording that changes what it would entail if left unrestricted, that wording must be given effect. It is impermissible to detach the statement from the qualifications joined to it. This, too, is undisputed among jurists—indeed, among all rational people.

Upon all this rest the rulings relating to the statements of legally accountable persons in matters of worship and transactions, such as endowments, bequests, acknowledgments, sales, gifts, pledges, leases, partnerships, and other matters.

Hence the jurists say: the founder’s wording determines whether an endowment is unrestricted or restricted.

Thus, if the opening words are unrestricted or general, and the speaker joins to them something that limits their scope or qualifies them, effect must be given to that qualification or limitation. If, for example, he says, “I establish an endowment for my children,” this is general. But if he adds “the poor,” “the upright,” or “the males,” the endowment is confined to them, even though his opening words were general.

Both those who affirm implication and those who deny it call this “connected specification.” They say: when the general wording is joined to a particular description, the ruling becomes attached exclusively to that description, and those who do not meet it are excluded from the ruling.

For those who deny implication, this is because such people would have no entitlement unless they were included in the wording. When the general wording was joined to the particular description, it excluded them from its scope. They therefore were not included and have no entitlement. Thus, they deny their entitlement because there is no basis for it.

Those who affirm implication exclude them on this ground and on another: specifically mentioning one of the two categories indicates an intention to confine the ruling to it, and intending to confine the ruling to them necessarily entails denying it to others. Thus, they deny their entitlement both because its basis is absent and because an impediment to it exists.

The same applies if he qualifies unrestricted wording, as when he says: “I establish an endowment for my children, on condition that they receive distributions if they are poor”; or “on condition that they are entitled if they are poor”; or “I establish an endowment for my children, on condition that distributions from the endowment are made to those of them who are living if they are poor”; or “I establish an endowment on condition that whoever is poor shall be among its beneficiaries.”

This is equivalent to saying: “I establish an endowment for my children—for the poor among them”; or “on condition that they are poor”; or “if he is poor.”

“I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you serve me for eight years.”

The jurists agree that if someone says, “I give you my daughter in marriage for a thousand,” or “on condition that you give her a thousand,” or “on condition that you owe her a thousand,” this constitutes a binding stipulation, and the specified dower is valid. There is no disagreement about this. Whoever believes that there is disagreement on this point in the school of Imam Ahmad or any other imam is mistaken. This misconception arises from their disagreement concerning someone who says to his wife, “You are divorced in return for a thousand,” or to his slave, “You are free in return for a thousand,” when the wife or slave does not accept. According to one of the two reports from Ahmad, the emancipation and divorce take effect. The basis for this is not that this expression does not convey a condition.

For there is no disagreement within his school that if someone says, “I release you from the marriage in return for a thousand,” “I enter into an emancipation contract with you for a thousand,” “I contract your marriage for a thousand,” “I sell you this slave on condition that you pledge such-and-such to me as security for its price,” “on condition that Zayd guarantees its payment,” or “I give you my daughter in marriage on condition that you are a free man,” these are valid stipulations. There is no disagreement about this among any of the jurists.

Rather, the reasoning is that emancipation and divorce do not require compensation, and that he has not made the divorce contingent upon a condition, but has merely attached a stipulation to it. A distinction is drawn between making an act contingent upon a condition and attaching a stipulation to a declaration that takes immediate effect. Once it is clear that his statement, “on condition that whoever among them dies,” constitutes a legally operative condition and a substantive qualification of the aforementioned endowment, and that it must be taken into account and acted upon, then the following is evident: taking this qualification into account makes the transfer of the deceased’s share to those of his generation conditional upon his leaving no child, and the founder did not assign the deceased’s share to them in this circumstance. It is then evident that the deceased’s share may not be allocated to them in the opposite circumstance, namely, when he leaves a child. This is precisely the point to be established.

It is also clear that this is agreed upon by the jurists—indeed, by rational people, whether they accept or reject arguments from implication. Allocating an endowment to anyone other than those to whom its founder assigned it is forbidden, and he did not assign it to them. This prohibition, based on the absence of grounds for entitlement, is unanimously accepted. Another ground is that he has prohibited its allocation to them; this prohibition, based on the existence of a preventive factor, is disputed.

The wording thus amounts to:

“I establish this endowment for my children, then for their children, on condition that the share of any deceased beneficiary passes to those of his generation if he dies leaving no child.”

No jurist disputes the restrictive effect of all the stated qualifications in this area. The only person who errs here is one who has not given due weight to the linguistic meanings of words, has not distinguished between the different categories of textually grounded principles of jurisprudence, and has not acquired experience in the rulings of Islamic law attached to the statements of legally accountable persons

and who, in understanding this discourse, has not followed the natural instincts of an Arabic speaker and a sound, uncorrupted disposition. He has risen above the level of ordinary people, no longer sharing their understanding of customary speech, yet fallen below the heights of the learned. Thus he has not learned to distinguish between deceptively similar expressions, so that innate dispositions may remain as they were fashioned by Him Who perfected everything He created; and folly has led him to escape from the refuse heap of Batrā.

Whoever masters the sciences and comprehends their furthest reaches is thereby brought back to affirming innate dispositions in their original state. The messengers were sent only to perfect the innate disposition, not to change it:

“The natural disposition Allah has instilled in mankind. There is no altering Allah’s creation.”

It is well known that all Arabic speakers who hear this statement, learned and ordinary alike, understand it only as assigning the share to those of the deceased’s generation on condition that he leaves no child. They recognize that this is a single, connected statement whose parts belong together. The mistaken interpreter’s error arose only because he imagined that the first clause was general in scope, while the second singled out one of the two categories for mention, thus making this a case of “conflict between general wording and implication.”

He may also have read the works of certain speculative theologians or jurists who do not accept arguments from implication, or who, if they accept them, consider the indication of general wording stronger. This is because opposition to the former is weaker than opposition to the latter: only an insignificant handful, whose views carry no weight, have disputed the validity of general wording, whereas the validity of implication has been disputed by a group of jurists

and groups of speculative theologians. Someone influenced by this may even imagine that he should not abandon the explicit wording of the condition, or its general scope, for the weaker implication of a qualifying attribute. We seek refuge in Allah from blindness of insight, or from a squint that makes one see a single thing as two. For a blind person’s perception is safer than that of someone with a squint if he follows a sighted person whose perception is sound. Were it not for the fear that someone might suppose this view to be tenable, or valid according to the principles of certain jurists, it would have been better to refrain from explaining it.

The answer is as follows:

The debate over whether implication constitutes authoritative evidence, and, if so, whether it can restrict the scope of general wording, concerns only two separate statements made by a single speaker, or treated as coming from a single speaker. It does not concern a single, connected statement whose parts belong together, nor statements made by two speakers whose intentions need not coincide. There are therefore three cases.

The first is two statements made by a single speaker, or treated as coming from a single speaker. We have included this latter qualification to cover cases in which one statement is Allah’s speech and the other is His Messenger’s. Such a case is treated just as though both statements were Allah’s speech or both were His Messenger’s speech.

An example is the Prophet’s statement, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure,”

together with his statement:

“When water reaches two qullahs (large jars), it does not become impure.”

Both were uttered by the same speaker, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, but they are two separate statements.

Thus, whoever holds that implication constitutes authoritative evidence by which general wording may be restricted restricts the general scope of his statement:

“Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure,”

by the implication of:

“When water reaches two qullahs, it does not become impure,”

even though the implication of a numerical specification

is weaker than the implication of a qualifying attribute. This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad—according to the well-known report from him—and others.

Those who reject this approach argue that his statement, “Water is purifying,” is general, while his statement, “When water reaches two qullahs, it does not become impure,” concerns a particular instance covered by that general wording and accords with its ruling. The general wording’s indication should therefore not be set aside on this account.

The same applies to his statement in the document on zakat issued by Abū Bakr:

“For camels, one sheep is due for every five,”

and the remainder of that passage, alongside his statement in another hadith:

“For grazing camels, a two-year-old she-camel is due for every forty, and a three-year-old she-camel for every fifty.”

There are many similar examples. In some, the scholars have agreed that the implication takes precedence, such as his statement:

“The earth has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification,”

alongside his statement:

“Every part of the earth that is pure has been made for me a place of prayer and a means of purification.”

There is no disagreement that impure earth is not a means of purification.

In other cases, they have differed, as with his statement in this hadith:

“And its soil has been made for me a means of purification.”

Al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others held that the implication of this hadith restricts the general scope of his statement:

“Every part of the earth that is pure has been made for me a means of purification.”

In still other cases, they have agreed that the general wording takes precedence, such as His statement:

“Do not approach the orphan’s property except in the way that is best,”

alongside His statement:

“Do not consume it wastefully and in haste lest they grow up.”

Consuming it is forbidden whether or not one intends to use it up before the orphan comes of age.

Scholars have differed over these two kinds of indication when they conflict. Thus, the proponents of juristic reasoning, the literalists, many speculative theologians, and a group of Mālikī and Shāfiʿī scholars

The majority of Mālikī, Shāfiʿī, and Hanbalī scholars, together with a group of speculative theologians, favored giving precedence to the implication. This is explicitly reported from al-Shāfiʿī, Ahmad, and others. The issue is open to debate, and this is not the place to discuss it in detail, for it has many ramifications. It is connected with the question of “unrestricted and qualified wording,” a deep sea within legal theory whose various forms have perplexed many who swim in its waters.

The point, however, is that the issue before us does not fall into this category. Even if it did, anyone issuing fatwas according to the schools of al-Shāfiʿī and Ahmad would be obliged to base this issue on their principles and those of their followers, rather than on principles formulated by certain speculative theologians. These theologians have not thoroughly examined Allah’s signs and the proofs He has explained in His Book and through His Messenger. Nor have they comprehensively understood the aspects and subtleties of the evidence Allah has placed in the revelation He sent down, or mastered the ways in which meaning is conveyed by the clearest of languages—the language in which Allah revealed the noblest of books.

Rather, this issue belongs to the second category: a single, continuous statement whose parts are connected, with its ending qualifying its beginning. An example would be to say:

“Water is purifying; nothing renders it impure when it reaches two qullahs.”

“One sheep is due for every five camels, and two sheep for ten. This zakat is obligatory on grazing camels.”

Likewise, Allah said:

“And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women…”

He initially left the wording unrestricted and general, then said at the end:

“That is for those of you who fear falling into sin.”

There is no disagreement that such a statement is not understood according to the general scope of its opening words. Rather, it establishes only the purity of water amounting to two qullahs or more, and the obligation of zakat on grazing camels.

However, those who reject the authority of implication say: “The statement neither affirms nor denies the ruling in other cases. We therefore deny it in those cases on the basis of the default presumption, unless evidence establishes a departure from that presumption.” The majority say: “Rather, we deny it on the evidence furnished by this statement, which accords with the default presumption.”

The distinction between connected and separate statements can be illustrated by a man saying: “I bequeath this wealth to the scholars; they are to receive from it if they are poor.” Alternatively, he might say on one occasion, “I bequeath it to the scholars,” and then say, “Give from my wealth to the scholars if they are poor.” In the latter case, one may speak of a conflict between the general wording and the implication.

Such a situation, however, does not arise with an endowment. Once a person establishes an endowment for beneficiaries described in general or specific terms, he cannot change those terms, unlike a bequest. Moreover, if a testator explains his wording in a way that differs from its apparent meaning, his explanation is accepted, unlike that of the founder of an endowment.

This is why we have said that restricting this statement by the qualification appearing at its end is obligatory according to everyone, both those who recognize the authority of implication and those who reject it. This does not belong to that category at all; rather, it is a statement restricted by a qualification at its end.

The third category:

This concerns statements made by different speakers whose intentions need not coincide. For example, two witnesses testify that an entire house belongs to Zayd, while two others testify that a particular part of it belongs to ‘Amr. These two sets of testimony conflict concerning that part. No one says that the general testimony should here be construed in light of the specific testimony. Someone once erred in a case of this kind, thinking that the two sets of testimony could be reconciled because this was a matter of general and specific wording, just as others erred concerning the second category by treating it as belonging to the first.

Those whose hearts Allah has illuminated distinguish between these three categories and recognize that the distinction between them is firmly rooted in everyone’s natural understanding. The distinctive role of scholars is simply to make explicit what is implicit. Even if we concede that the initial wording is general or unrestricted, it has been directly joined to wording that qualifies it and limits its scope. All rational people agree that wording of this kind is qualified and limited in scope, neither general nor unrestricted.

There is thus a difference—may Allah set you right—between completing a general, unrestricted statement and then falling silent, after which an implication with a specific or qualified scope conflicts with it, and directly joining that statement to wording that qualifies it and limits its scope. Do you not know that all rulings rest on this distinction? If someone swears an oath, remains silent for a long time, and then appends an exception, a coordinated phrase, a qualification, or something else of that kind, it has no effect.

For example, suppose he says, “By Allah, I will not travel,” then remains silent for a long time before saying, “If Allah wills”; or says, “To such-and-such a place”; or says, “Nor will I marry”; or says, “I will not travel on foot.” The oath is not qualified by any of this.

Likewise, if he swears on one occasion, “I will not travel,” and then swears on a second occasion that he will not travel on foot, no restriction would thereby be imposed

One mistake some minds make in such cases is to suppose that the beginning of a statement contradicts or conflicts with its ending. This is one of the specious objections raised by some of the linguistically inept among those who deny that wording can have general application. They say:

“If these forms of expression were general, an exception would constitute a retraction or a contradiction.”

This is ignorance. Numerical expressions are unambiguous, yet they admit exceptions, as Allah Most High says:

“So he remained among them a thousand years, less fifty.”

Likewise, an indefinite noun in an affirmative statement is unrestricted, yet it admits qualification, as in His words:

“Then the freeing of a slave.”

Their error arises from imagining that to describe these forms of expression as general is to describe them as unconditionally general. If they are said to be unconditionally general, and an exception then removes part of what they entail, the excluded case would be both included by the general expression and excluded by the exception. That, they argue, would constitute a contradiction or a retraction.

The answer is:

“When these expressions are described as general, their general application is conditional upon their not being connected to a clause that restricts their scope. Thus, they are general when left unqualified, not general without qualification. The same expression conveys different meanings depending on whether it is left unqualified or qualified.”

For this reason, the jurists unanimously agree that if a man were to say, “I owe him a thousand dirhams in such-and-such coinage,” or “in broken coins

or black coins, or underweight ones, or coins of Tiberias,” or “a thousand less fifty,” or the like, his acknowledgement would be subject to that specific qualification. If an exception constituted a retraction, it would not be accepted in an acknowledgement, since a person may not retract an acknowledgement concerning the rights of others.

Some marginal jurists frequently err in such matters. When asked about a condition stipulated by the founder of an endowment, an oath someone has sworn, or something similar, a jurist sees that the opening words are unrestricted or general, while their ending qualifies them. Sometimes he treats this as a conflict between two pieces of evidence, applying the familiar rules governing conflicting evidence, such as judging them equally strong or giving one precedence. Sometimes he regards the statement as contradictory because its ending differs from its beginning. At other times he flounders in bewilderment, attributing to a capable person the conduct of someone negligent. He may even say, “This is a mistake by the scribe.” All this stems from failing to distinguish between connected speech and separate statements.

Anyone who understands that a speaker’s opening words must not be judged until he has made a pause that definitively ends his statement, and that a writer’s text must not be judged until he has definitively finished writing, will be free of confusion in this matter and recognize the soundness of what scholars say about how discourse conveys meaning.

It is a grave failing to attribute an error to a speaker when his words admit a sound interpretation and follow the finest patterns of ordinary speech, and then to deem one of the two supposedly conflicting passages mistaken rather than the other. It is also astonishing to suppose that this is merely emphasis, when emphasis serves to dispel doubt. If the ruling were the same in both cases and emphasis were intended, “whoever among them dies leaving a child” would have been more appropriate than “whoever among them dies without leaving a child.” For transferring the deceased’s share to his brothers even when he leaves a child already indicates that it should pass to them when he leaves none. To provide emphasis by explaining the obvious ruling rather than the less obvious one is to overstep the bounds of reason and language.

Moreover, emphasis is not expressed through adjectives that restrict the scope of the nouns they qualify. If someone said, “Honor Muslim men,” then explained, “I intended all men to be honored; I singled out Muslims for emphasis, and mentioning them does not exclude others once they have been included under the first term,” this claim would be entirely untenable and unacceptable. For “Muslim” qualifies “men,” and an adjective restricts the scope of the noun it qualifies, leaving it no longer general.

But if he said, “Honor men and Muslims”—using a conjunction, with the same instruction applying to both groups and Muslims being a subset of men—this would constitute emphasis. For a conjoined term does not necessarily restrict or narrow the term to which it is joined, owing to the distinction created between them by the conjunction, unlike adjectives

 إنَّمَا فُهِمَ الْمَعْنَى هُنَا بِمَجْمُوعِ قَوْلِهِ: أَلْفٌ إلَّا خَمْسِينَ؛ لَا بِنَفْسِ الْأَلْفِ. فَصَارَتْ هَذِهِ الْأَلْفَاظُ الثَّلَاثَةُ هِيَ الدَّالَّةُ عَلَى تِسْعِمِائَةٍ وَخَمْسِينَ. وَهَذِهِ شُبْهَةُ مَنْ رَأَى أَنَّ الْعَامَّ الْمَخْصُوصَ تَخْصِيصًا مُتَّصِلًا مَجَازٌ. كَالْعَامِّ الْمَخْصُوصِ تَخْصِيصًا مُنْفَصِلًا عِنْدَ كَثِيرٍ مِنْ النَّاسِ
translated_text:
and similar qualifiers, which do restrict meaning; so do certain kinds of conjunction. This, however, is not the place to discuss that distinction in detail. Hence, in their discussions of acknowledgments, divorce, and contracts, jurists distinguish between conjunctions that alter the preceding meaning and those that do not.

Anyone who seeks to assign a valid meaning to an utterance before it is complete must regard the beginning of the declaration of Allah’s oneness as disbelief and its ending as faith, and hold that the person uttering it has disbelieved and then believed. We seek refuge in Allah from such folly.

It has, indeed, been related that someone asked, “What declaration begins with disbelief and ends with faith?” When asked, “What is it?” he replied, “The declaration of pure faith.” I say: He meant that its beginning would constitute disbelief if the speaker stopped there. He did not mean that it constitutes disbelief when joined to the exception; had he meant that, he would have committed disbelief.

Hence, scholars of precise understanding have said, “Making an exception means speaking of what remains after the excepted portion is excluded.”

Some have mistakenly supposed that, when someone says, “A thousand except fifty,” the word “thousand” is used figuratively, because it is being used for something other than its assigned meaning: it denotes the number in its entirety, whereas the speaker did not intend that.

The reply is: That is its assigned meaning when it stands alone, without an attached qualification; that condition no longer holds here.

Furthermore, the meaning here is understood only from the complete expression, “A thousand except fifty,” not from “thousand” alone. Thus, these three terms together signify nine hundred and fifty. This is the misconception underlying the view that a general expression restricted by an attached qualification is figurative, just as many people regard a general expression restricted by a separate qualification as figurative.

" حَقِيقَةً أَوْ مَجَازًا "

" بَابِ الْوُقُوفِ "

translated_text:
And the implications of this view are that every noun or verb accompanied by an adjective, an explanatory apposition, a substitute, any qualifying complement, a circumstantial qualifier, an accusative of specification, or the like would be used figuratively. This is self-evidently false. The distinction between an attached verbal indicator that signifies by linguistic convention, other indicators—whether circumstantial or verbal—that do not convey the intended meaning by linguistic convention, as in “I saw a lion writing and an ocean sailing on the sea,” and separate expressions is known with certainty in the languages of Arabs and non-Arabs alike.

Nevertheless, no rational person doubts that an utterance is complete only when it reaches its end, and that its meaning can be understood only after it is complete in its entirety. Its beginning cannot convey its meaning independently of its ending, whether that beginning is called “literal or figurative.” Nor may it be said that its beginning contradicts its ending. Contradiction can arise only between two independent proofs, whereas a connected utterance in its entirety constitutes a single proof. To posit a contradiction between its parts is like positing a contradiction between the parts of compound names.

This is clear, particularly in “the subject of endowments.” The founder of an endowment may wish to stipulate numerous conditions concerning the endowed property and its beneficiaries—joint or successive entitlement, equal or preferential allocation, and unrestricted or restricted provisions—enough to fill a lengthy document. Yet no Muslim has disputed that it is impermissible to treat the beginning of his statement as unrestricted and general while disregarding its ending, or to regard the restrictions, details, and specifications at the end of his statement as contradicting or conflicting with what came at the outset

فَإِنْ قِيلَ:

 كَالْأَقْوَالِ الثَّلَاثَةِ فِي قَوْلِهِ:
 عَلَى أَوْلَادِي الثَّلَاثَةِ ثُمَّ عَلَى الْمَسَاكِينِ. أَحَدُهَا - وَهُوَ الْمَشْهُورُ -
 أَنَّهُ يَكُونُ لِلْبَاقِينَ مِنْ الطَّبَقَةِ الْعُلْيَا وَالثَّانِي:
 أَنَّهُ يَنْتَقِلُ إلَى الطَّبَقَةِ الثَّانِيَةِ؛ كَمَا لَوْ انْقَرَضَتْ الطَّبَقَةُ الْعُلْيَا.
translated_text:
in the form of unrestricted or general terms. This is like a man examining an endowment whose founder had said, “I endow this for my children, then for their children,” and subsequently added, “One condition for the beneficiaries is that they be poor, upright in character, or the like.” The man then says, “This statement is self-contradictory, because at its beginning he endowed it for everyone, which contradicts restricting it to some.” He then treats this as a matter of “the specific and the general” and “conflicting proofs.”

It is clear that all this is confused reasoning. For a conflict presupposes that each proof independently conveys its meaning, and such independence presupposes that the statement has ended and stands separately. When, however, it remains connected to wording that changes its effect, one part cannot be treated as proof contradicting another. May Allah, glorified be He, guide us and all Muslims to what He loves and is pleased with.

If it is said: His wording, “on condition that whoever among them dies,” may be a condition stipulated by the founder to clarify that the endowment passes to those who remain and that it does not suffer an interruption midway. For some jurists have derived three opinions concerning what happens when one beneficiary dies under the stipulation, “For my children, then for my children’s children,” corresponding to the three opinions concerning the stipulation, “For my three children, then for the poor.” The first—and it is the well-known opinion—is that it belongs to the remaining members of the first tier. The second is that it passes to the second tier, as though all members of the first tier had died.

original_text:
وَالثَّالِثُ:

 قُلْنَا:
 سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ الْعَظِيمِ هَذَا كَلَامُ مَنْ قَدْ نَأَى عَنْ مَوْضِعِ اسْتِدْلَالِنَا. فَإِنَّا لَمْ نَسْتَدِلَّ بِصِيغَةِ الشَّرْطِ الْمُطْلَقَةِ؛ وَإِنَّمَا اسْتَدْلَلْنَا بِمَا تَضَمَّنَهُ الشَّرْطُ مِنْ التَّقْيِيدِ؛
 فَإِنَّ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ جَيِّدٌ لَوْ كَانَ الْوَاقِفُ قَالَ:
 عَلَى أَنَّهُ مَنْ مَاتَ مِنْهُمْ انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهُ إلَى ذَوِي طَبَقَتِهِ. وَلَوْ قَالَ هَذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ فِي الْمَسْأَلَةِ شُبْهَةٌ أَنَّ نَصِيبَ الْمَيِّتِ يَنْتَقِلُ إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ مَعَ الْوَلَدِ وَعَدَمِهِ مِنْ وُجُوهٍ مُتَعَدِّدَةٍ.
 مِنْهَا:
 أَنَّ هَذَا هُوَ مُوجَبُ الْكَلَامِ الْأَوَّلِ عِنْدَ الْإِطْلَاقِ وَلَمْ يُوصَلْ بِمَا يُغَيِّرُهُ.
 وَمِنْهَا:
 أَنَّهُ وَصَلَ بِمَا وَكَّدَ مُوجِبَ مُطْلَقِهِ.
 وَمِنْهَا:
 أَنَّهُ قَدْ شَرَطَ ذَلِكَ شَرْطًا نَفَى بِهِ الصَّرْفَ إلَى الطَّبَقَةِ الثَّانِيَةِ وَنَفَى بِهِ الِانْقِطَاعَ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ لِلْمَيِّتِ وَلَدٌ أَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ.
 وَإِنَّمَا صُورَةُ مَسْأَلَتِنَا أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 عَلَى أَنَّهُ مَنْ تُوُفِّيَ مِنْهُمْ عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ
translated_text:
And the third is that its disposition is left unspecified, resulting in an interruption midway through the endowment, as if he had said: “I endow it for Zayd, and, ten years after his death, for the poor.” Since an interruption midway upon the death of one beneficiary is a possible interpretation, the founder included this condition to exclude that possibility, even though, according to the first opinion, this condition merely expresses what the endowment already entails. Some conditions accord with what the wording already implies and thus serve to reinforce its effect.

We reply: Glory be to Allah, the Magnificent! These are the words of someone who has strayed far from the point of our argument. We did not base our argument on the bare formulation of a condition, but on the restriction contained within it. This objection would indeed be sound had the founder said: “On condition that whoever among them dies, his share shall pass to the members of his tier.” Had he said this, there would have been no doubt that the deceased’s share passes to the members of his tier, whether or not he leaves a child, for several reasons.

First, this is what the initial wording entails when left unrestricted, and nothing modifying its effect has been appended to it.

Second, he has appended wording that reinforces what his unrestricted statement entails.

Third, he has expressly stipulated this in a condition that excludes both transfer to the second tier and any interruption, whether or not the deceased leaves a child.

The actual case before us, however, is that he said: “On condition that whoever among them dies leaving no child

 وَقَفْت عَلَى أَوْلَادِي الثَّلَاثَةِ ثُمَّ عَلَى الْمَسَاكِينِ: عَلَى أَنَّهُ مَنْ مَاتَ مِنْهُمْ فِي حَيَاةِ الْوَاقِفِ صُرِفَ نَصِيبُهُ إلَى مَنْ فِي دَرَجَتِهِ. فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَصْرِفَ نَصِيبَهُ إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ إذَا مَاتَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِ الْوَاقِفِ. هَذَا لَمْ يَقُلْهُ أَحَدٌ فِي هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ؛
 لَكِنْ قَدْ يُقَالُ:
 إنَّهُ مَسْكُوتٌ عَنْ مَوْتِهِ بَعْدَ مَوْتِ الْوَاقِفِ فَيَكُونُ مُنْقَطِعَ الْوَسَطِ.
 وَالصَّوَابُ الَّذِي عَلَيْهِ النَّاسُ قَدِيمًا وَحَدِيثًا:
 أَنَّهُ يَكُونُ لِلْمَسَاكِينِ لِأَنَّ اللَّفْظَ اقْتَضَى جَعْلَهُ لِلثَّلَاثَةِ؛ ثُمَّ لِلْمَسَاكِينِ فَحَيْثُ لَمْ يَصْرِفْ إلَى الثَّلَاثَةِ تَعَيَّنَ صَرْفُهُ إلَى الْمَسَاكِينِ لِحَصْرِ الْوَاقِفِ الْوَقْفَ فِيهَا مَعَ أَنَّ بَحْثَ مَسْأَلَتِنَا أَظْهَرُ مِنْ هَذِهِ كَمَا تَقَدَّمَ؛
 بَلْ لَوْ فُرِضَ أَنَّ قَائِلًا قَدْ قَالَ:
 إذَا مَاتَ عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ يَكُونُ مُنْقَطِعًا وَإِذَا مَاتَ عَنْ وَلَدٍ لَمْ يَكُنْ: لَجَازَ أَنْ يُقَالَ: هَذَا الشَّرْطُ لِنَفْيِ احْتِمَالِ الِانْقِطَاعِ وَمَعَ هَذَا فَهُوَ دَالٌّ عَلَى التَّقْيِيدِ كَمَا ذَكَرْنَاهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَدُلُّ عَلَى صَرْفِ نَصِيبِ الْمَيِّتِ عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ إلَى طَبَقَتِهِ وَعَلَى عَدَمِ الصَّرْفِ إلَيْهِمْ مَعَ الْوَلَدِ. فَالدَّلَالَةُ الْأُولَى تَنْفِي الِانْقِطَاعَ وَالدَّلَالَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ تُوجِبُ الِاشْتِرَاكَ وَلَا مُنَافَاةَ بَيْنَهُمَا.
translated_text:
or grandchild, or any progeny or descendants, his share shall pass to the members of his tier.” Thus, he made its transfer to them conditional upon the deceased leaving no child. Just as this condition excludes an interruption, it also restricts transfer to the members of that tier. The wording explicitly conveys both meanings; its conveying one does not prevent it from conveying the other.

This is like saying: “I endow it for my three children, then for the poor, on condition that whoever among them dies during the founder’s lifetime, his share shall be assigned to those of his own tier.” Would it then be permissible to assign his share to the members of his tier if he dies after the founder’s death? No one has held this in such a case. It might, however, be said that his dying after the founder’s death is left unaddressed, so that the endowment has an interruption midway.

The correct view, held in earlier times and today, is that his share passes to the poor. The wording assigns it to the three, then to the poor; whenever it is not assigned to the three, it must therefore be assigned to the poor, since the founder confined the endowment to these beneficiaries. Moreover, the argument in our case is clearer still, as explained above.

Indeed, even supposing someone had said that if he dies leaving no child there is an interruption, whereas if he dies leaving a child there is none, one could say that this condition serves to exclude the possibility of interruption. Nevertheless, it also conveys a restriction, as we have explained: it indicates that the share of someone who dies leaving no child is to be assigned to his tier, and that it is not to be assigned to them when he leaves a child. The first implication excludes interruption, while the second requires shared entitlement. There is no incompatibility between the two.

original_text:
بَلْ الْأُولَى حَصَلَتْ مِنْ وَضْعِ هَذَا اللَّفْظِ وَالثَّانِيَةُ حَصَلَتْ مِنْ مَجْمُوعِ الشَّرْطِ أَوْ الْكَلَامِ الْأَوَّلِ؛ فَكَيْفَ وَالْأَمْرُ لَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ.
 فَإِنْ قِيلَ:
 هَذَا نَفْيٌ لِلِاحْتِمَالِ فِي هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ وَإِنْ كَانَ لَمْ يَنْفِهِ فِي أُخْرَى قُلْنَا: هَذَا إنَّمَا يَسْتَقِيمُ أَنْ لَوْ لَمْ تَكُنْ الصُّورَةُ الْمَذْكُورَةُ مُقَيِّدَةٌ لِلَّفْظِ الْمُطْلَقِ فَإِنَّ قَوْلَهُ: مَنْ مَاتَ مِنْهُمْ.
 مُطْلَقٌ وَقَدْ قَيَّدَهُ:
 عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ.
 وَفِي مِثْلِ هَذَا لَا يُقَالُ:
 ذَكَرَ صُورَةً وَتَرَكَ أُخْرَى؛ إلَّا إذَا كَانَ الْكَلَامُ مُسْتَقِلًّا بِنَفْسِهِ غَيْرَ مُتَّصِلٍ بِغَيْرِهِ؛ فَأَمَّا إذَا كَانَ الْكَلَامُ مُتَّصِلًا بِغَيْرِهِ فَإِنَّهُ يَصِيرُ قَيْدًا فِي ذَلِكَ الْأَوَّلِ؛
 فَإِنَّ قَوْلَهُ:
 عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ. نُصِبَ عَلَى الْحَالِ أَيْضًا؛
 وَالْحَالُ صِفَةٌ وَالصِّفَةُ مُقَيِّدَةٌ فَكَأَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 بِشَرْطِ أَنَّهُ مَنْ كَانَ مَوْتُهُ عَلَى هَذِهِ الصِّفَةِ انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهُ إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ؛ أَوْ أَنَّهُ يَنْتَقِلُ نَصِيبُ الْمَيِّتِ إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ بِشَرْطِ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ لِلْمَيِّتِ وَلَدٌ وَمَعْلُومٌ بِالِاضْطِرَارِ أَنَّ الِانْتِقَالَ الْمَشْرُوطَ بِصِفَةِ لَا يَجُوزُ إثْبَاتُهُ بِدُونِ تِلْكَ الصِّفَةِ.
 فَقَوْلُهُ:
 عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ. صِفَةٌ لِمَوْتِ الْمَيِّتِ؛
 وَالِانْتِقَالُ إذَا مَاتَ الْمَيِّتُ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْحَالِ صِفَةٌ لِلْوَقْفِ وَالْوَقْفُ الْمَوْصُوفُ بِصِفَةِ وَتِلْكَ الصِّفَةُ مَوْصُوفَةٌ بِأُخْرَى:
 لَا يَجُوزُ إثْبَاتُهُ إلَّا مَعَ وُجُودِ الصِّفَةِ وَصِفَةِ الصِّفَةِ. فَلَا يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَكُونَ وَقْفًا عَلَى الْأَوْلَادِ؛ ثُمَّ أَوْلَادُهُمْ؛ إلَّا بِشَرْطِ انْتِقَالِ نَصِيبِ الْمُتَوَفَّى إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ.
translated_text:
Rather, the first implication follows from the conventional meaning of this wording, while the second follows from the condition taken as a whole or from the opening statement. How much more so when matters are not as supposed!

If it is said, “This excludes that possibility in this case, even though it does not exclude it in another,” we reply: This would hold only if the case mentioned did not restrict the unrestricted wording. His statement, “Whoever among them dies,” is unrestricted, but he has restricted it by saying, “leaving no child.” In such a construction, one cannot say, “He mentioned one case and left another unaddressed,” unless the statement stands independently, unconnected to anything else. When it is connected to another statement, however, it becomes a restriction upon that preceding statement.

The phrase “leaving no child” is also construed as a circumstantial qualifier in the accusative. A circumstantial qualifier is descriptive, and a description restricts the scope. It is therefore as though he said, “On condition that whoever dies in this state, his share shall pass to the members of his tier”; or, “The deceased’s share shall pass to the members of his tier on condition that he leaves no child.” It is self-evident that a transfer made conditional upon a particular qualification cannot be affirmed in the absence of that qualification.

Thus, “leaving no child” describes the circumstances of the deceased’s death. The transfer, when the deceased dies in this state, is a qualification of the endowment. When an endowment has a qualification, and that qualification is itself further qualified, the endowment cannot be affirmed except where both the qualification and its further qualification are present. Thus, it cannot be an endowment for the children, then their children, except on condition that the deceased’s share passes to the members of his tier.

original_text:
وَلَا يَجُوزُ نَقْلُ نَصِيبِ الْمَيِّتِ إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ إلَّا بِشَرْطِ مَوْتِهِ عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ أَوْ وَلَدِ وَلَدٍ أَوْ نَسْلٍ أَوْ عَقِبٍ؛ حَتَّى لَوْ كَانَ لَهُ وَلَدٌ - وَإِنْ بَعُدَ -
 كَانَ وُجُودُهُ مَانِعًا مِنْ الِانْتِقَالِ إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ وَمُوجِبًا لِلِانْتِقَالِ إلَيْهِ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 عَلَى أَوْلَادِهِ ثُمَّ أَوْلَادِ أَوْلَادِهِ. ثُمَّ نَسْلِهِ وَعَقِبِهِ دَائِمًا مَا تَنَاسَلُوا. وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ هَذَا السُّؤَالَ لَا يَكَادُ يَنْضَبِطُ وُجُوهُ فَسَادِهِ مَعَ مَا ذَكَرْنَاهُ. لِكَثْرَتِهَا.
 مِنْهَا:
 أَنَّهُ لَوْ كَانَ قَصْدُهُ مُجَرَّدَ نَفْيِ احْتِمَالِ الِانْقِطَاعِ لَكَانَ التَّعْمِيمُ بِقَوْلِهِ: مَنْ مَاتَ مِنْهُمْ انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهُ.
 أَوْ التَّنْبِيهُ بِقَوْلِهِ:
 مَنْ مَاتَ مِنْهُمْ عَنْ وَلَدٍ انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهُ إلَى ذَوِي طَبَقَتِهِ. هُوَ الْوَاجِبُ؛ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهُ إلَى ذَوِي الطَّبَقَةِ مَعَ الْوَلَدِ فَمَعَ عَدَمِهِ أَوْلَى.
 أَمَّا أَنْ يَنُصَّ عَلَى انْتِقَالِهِ إلَى الطَّبَقَةِ مَعَ عَدَمِ الْوَلَدِ نَافِيًا بِذَلِكَ احْتِمَالَ الِانْقِطَاعِ ثُمَّ يُرِيدُ مِنَّا أَنْ نَفْهَمَ انْتِقَالَهُ إلَيْهِمْ أَيْضًا مَعَ الْوَلَدِ لِمُجَرَّدِ قَوْلِهِ:
 عَلَى وَلَدِي ثُمَّ وَلَدِ وَلَدِي. مَعَ أَنَّ احْتِمَالَ الِانْقِطَاعِ هُنَا قَائِمٌ مَعَ احْتِمَالٍ آخَرَ يَنْفَرِدُ بِهِ وَهُوَ الِانْتِقَالُ إلَى الْوَلَدِ؛
 لِأَنَّ احْتِمَالَ انْتِقَالِهِ إلَى وَلَدِ الْوَلَدِ هُنَا أَظْهَرُ مِنْ احْتِمَالِ الِانْقِطَاعِ وَمَعَ أَنَّ فَهْمَ التَّخْصِيصِ مَعَ التَّقْيِيدِ أَظْهَرُ مِنْ فَهْمِ الِانْقِطَاعِ وَمَعَ أَنَّ دَلَالَةَ قَوْلِهِ:
 عَلَى وَلَدِ وَلَدِي. فِي الِانْتِقَالِ إلَى الطَّبَقَةِ مَعَ عَدَمِ الْوَلَدِ أَظْهَرُ مِنْ دَلَالَتِهِ فِي الِانْتِقَالِ إلَيْهِمْ مَعَ وُجُودِ الْوَلَدِ. فَقَدْ أَرَادَ مِنَّا أَنْ نَفْهَمَ الْكَلَامَ الْمَقْلُوبَ وَنَخْرُجَ عَنْ حُدُودِ الْعَقْلِ وَالْبَيَانِ؛ فَإِنَّ
translated_text:
and the deceased’s share may not pass to the members of his tier unless he dies leaving no child, grandchild, offspring, or posterity. Thus, if he has a descendant—even a remote one—that descendant’s existence prevents the share from passing to the members of his tier and requires it to pass instead to that descendant, by virtue of the founder’s words: “For his children, then his children’s children, then his offspring and posterity, perpetually, for as long as they continue to have descendants.”

Know that, beyond what we have already mentioned, the flaws in this objection are almost too numerous to enumerate. Among them is the following: If his intention were merely to exclude the possibility of a lapse in the endowment, he would have had to use general wording, saying, “Whoever among them dies, his share shall pass on”; or draw attention to the implication by saying, “Whoever among them dies leaving a child, his share shall pass to the members of his tier.” For if his share passes to the members of his tier despite his having a child, then it should all the more do so when he has none.

But suppose he expressly states that the share passes to the members of the tier when there is no child, thereby excluding the possibility of a lapse, and then expects us to understand that it also passes to them when there is a child, merely because he said, “For my children, then my children’s children.” Here, however, the possibility of a lapse remains, alongside another possibility peculiar to this case: that the share passes to the deceased’s child. Indeed, the possibility of its passing to the founder’s grandchild here is more evident than the possibility of a lapse. Moreover, a restrictive reading, given the qualification, is more evident than the inference of a lapse. Furthermore, the words “For my children’s children” indicate more clearly that the share passes to the members of the tier when there is no child than that it passes to them when there is a child. He would thus be asking us to understand his words backwards and to step beyond the bounds of reason and clear expression. For

original_text:
تَرْكَهُ لِرَفْعِ احْتِمَالِ الِانْقِطَاعِ وَغَيْرِهِ فِيمَا هُوَ فِيهِ أَظْهَرُ؛ وَعُدُولُهُ عَنْ الْعِبَارَةِ الْمُحَقِّقَةِ لِنَفْيِ الِانْقِطَاعِ مُطْلَقًا بِلَا لَبْسٍ إلَى عِبَارَةٍ هِيَ فِي التَّقْيِيدِ أَظْهَرُ مِنْهَا فِي مُجَرَّدِ نَفْيِ انْقِطَاعِ بَعْضِ الصُّوَرِ دَلِيلٌ قَاطِعٌ عَلَى أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَقْصِدْ بِذَلِكَ.
 وَنَظِيرُ هَذَا رَجُلٌ قَالَ لِعَبْدِهِ:
 أَكْرِمْ زَيْدًا إنْ كَانَ رَجُلًا صَالِحًا فَأَكْرِمْهُ. وَكَانَ غَيْرَ صَالِحٍ فَلَمْ يُكْرِمْهُ الْغُلَامُ.
 فَقَالَ لَهُ سَيِّدُهُ:
 عَصَيْت أَمْرِي. أَلَمْ آمُرْك بِإِكْرَامِهِ؟
 قَالَ:
 قَدْ قُلْت لِي: إنْ كَانَ صَالِحًا فَأَكْرِمْهُ قَالَ: إنَّمَا قُلْت هَذَا لِئَلَّا تَتَوَهَّمَ أَنِّي أَبْغَضُ الصَّالِحِينَ فَلَا تُكْرِمْهُ مَعَ صَلَاحِهِ فَنَفَيْت احْتِمَالَ التَّخْصِيصِ فِي هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ.
 فَهَلْ يُقْبَلُ هَذَا الْكَلَامُ مِنْ عَاقِلٍ أَوْ يُنْسَبُ الْغُلَامُ إلَى تَفْرِيطٍ أَوْ يَقُولُ لِلسَّيِّدِ:
 هَذِهِ الْعِبَارَةُ دَالَّةٌ عَلَى التَّخْصِيصِ وَلَوْ كُنْت مُثْبِتًا لِلتَّعْمِيمِ لَكَانَ الْوَاجِبُ أَنْ تَقُولَ: أُكْرِمُهُ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ صَالِحًا؛ لِأَنَّ إكْرَامَ الصَّالِحِ يَصِيرُ مِنْ بَابِ التَّنْبِيهِ؛
 أَوْ أُكْرِمُهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ صَالِحًا إنْ كَانَ حُبًّا لَك صَحِيحًا وَكَذَا هُنَا يَقُولُ الْمُنَازِعُ:
 هُوَ نَقَلَهُ إلَى الطَّبَقَةِ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ لَهُ وَلَدٌ أَوْ لَمْ يَكُنْ.
 فَإِذَا قِيلَ لَهُ:
 فَلِمَ قَيَّدَ النَّقْلَ بِقَوْلِهِ: عَلَى أَنَّهُ مَنْ مَاتَ مِنْهُمْ عَنْ غَيْرِ وَلَدٍ انْتَقَلَ نَصِيبُهُ إلَى الطَّبَقَةِ؟
 قَالَ:
 لِيَنْفِيَ احْتِمَالَ الِانْقِطَاعِ فِي هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ دُونَ الصُّورَةِ الَّتِي هِيَ أَوْلَى بِنَفْيِ الِانْقِطَاعِ فِيهَا.
 فَيُقَالُ لَهُ:
 كَانَ الْكَلَامُ
translated_text:
his failure to dispel the possibility of a lapse and other possibilities where these are more apparent, and his departure from wording that would unequivocally exclude a lapse in every case, in favour of wording that more clearly indicates a restriction than merely excludes a lapse in certain cases, are conclusive evidence that this was not what he intended.

A parallel would be a man saying to his slave: “Honour Zayd. If he is righteous, honour him.” Zayd is not righteous, so the servant does not honour him. His master then says to him: “You have disobeyed my command. Did I not order you to honour him?”

The servant replies: “You told me: ‘If he is righteous, honour him.’”

The master says: “I only said this so that you would not imagine that I hate righteous people and therefore refrain from honouring him despite his righteousness. I was excluding the possibility of an exception in this particular case.”

Would such an explanation be accepted from a rational person? Would the servant be accused of negligence? Or would he say to his master: “This wording indicates a restriction. Had you intended the command to apply generally, you should have said: ‘Honour him even if he is not righteous,’ since honouring a righteous person would then follow all the more clearly; or: ‘Honour him even if he is righteous,’ if he is truly dear to you.”

Likewise, here the disputant says: “The founder transferred the share to the members of the tier, whether or not the deceased had a child.”

When asked, “Why, then, did he qualify the transfer by saying: ‘Provided that, if any of them dies leaving no child, his share shall pass to the members of the tier’?” he replies: “To exclude the possibility of a lapse in this case, but not in the case in which there is even greater reason to exclude it.”

expressed in Arabic in such a case as follows: ‘Provided that, if any of them dies, even if he has a child, his share shall pass to the members of his tier.’ Or he could say: ‘Provided that, if any of them dies, even if he has no child,’ thus including the conjunction.”

But if he says, “Provided that, if any of them dies leaving no child,” this explicitly establishes a restriction and admits no other interpretation. Whoever imagines otherwise, considers it even remotely possible, or considers it possible for a rational person to accept such an interpretation, has undoubtedly forfeited the blessing Allah bestowed upon mankind when He taught them expression. I do not think that, left to his innate disposition, he would imagine such a thing. Yet innate dispositions may suffer corrupting influences that impair their soundness, as the hadiths declare.

Another argument is that a rational person does not exclude a remote possibility by introducing a more apparent one. Clearly, had the founder omitted this condition, the possibility of a lapse would have been exceedingly remote: it either contradicts scholarly consensus or ranks among discredited juristic opinions. Once the condition is mentioned, however, restriction and an ordered distribution become a strong possibility—an apparent meaning even according to the disputant, and a conclusive one according to others. How, then, can the founder’s words be interpreted as following a blameworthy course rather than a commendable one, when the latter interpretation is possible?

Another argument is that only some jurists would notice this possibility; perhaps it has only recently arisen in Islamic history. The possibility of restriction, however, is a feature of language that existed before Islam.
