وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَمَّنْ أَوْقَفَ وَقْفًا عَلَى الْفُقَرَاءِ. وَهُوَ مِنْ كُرُومٍ يَحْصُلُ لِأَصْحَابِهَا ضَرَرٌ بِهِ. فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يَرْجِعَ فِيهِ وَيَقِفَ غَيْرَهُ؟ وَهَلْ إذَا فَعَلَ يَكُونُ الِاثْنَانِ وَقْفًا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا كَانَ فِي ذَلِكَ ضَرَر كُلّ الْجِيرَانِ جَاز أَنَّ يُنَاقِلُ عَنْهُ مَا يَقُومُ مَقَامه وَيَعُودُ الْأَوَّل مَلِكًا وَالثَّانِي وَقْفًا كَمَا فَعَلَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ فِي مَسْجِد الْكُوفَة لِمَا جَعَلَ مَكَانُهُ مَسْجِدًا صَارَ الْأَوَّل سُوقًا لِلتَّمَارِينِ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ حَوْضِ سَبِيلٍ وَعَلَيْهِ وَقْفُ إسْطَبْلٍ وَقَدْ بَاعَهُ النَّاظِرُ وَلَمْ يَشْتَرِ بِثَمَنِهِ شَيْئًا مِنْ مُدَّةِ سِتِّ سِنِينَ. فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، أَمَّا بَيْعُهُ بِغَيْرِ اسْتِبْدَالٍ لِمَا يَقُومُ مَقَامَهُ فَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّهُ لَا يَجُوزُ. وَأَمَّا إذَا بَاعَهُ لِتُعَطِّلْ نَفْعِهِ وَاشْتَرَى بِالثَّمَنِ مَا يَقُومُ مَقَامَهُ فَهَذَا يَجُوزُ عَلَى الصَّحِيحِ فِي قَوْلَيْ الْعُلَمَاءِ وَإِنْ اسْتَبْدَلَ بِهِ خَيْرًا مِنْهُ مَعَ وُجُودِ نَفْعِهِ فَفِيهِ نِزَاعٌ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

“Someone endowed property for the poor. It is part of a group of vineyards whose owners suffer harm because of the endowment. May he revoke it and endow something else instead? If he does so, do both properties become endowments?”

He replied:

“If this causes harm to all the neighbours, it is permissible to exchange it for property that serves the same purpose. The original property then reverts to private ownership, and the replacement becomes an endowment. This is what Umar ibn al-Khattāb, may Allah be pleased with him, did with the mosque of Kufa: when he established another mosque in its place, the original site became a market for date sellers.”

He was also asked:

“A stable was endowed to support a water basin provided for public use. The administrator sold the stable but has purchased nothing with the proceeds for six years. Is this permissible?”

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah. There is no doubt that selling it without acquiring a replacement that serves the same purpose is impermissible. However, if he sold it because it had ceased to be useful and purchased a replacement with the proceeds, this is permissible according to the sounder of the scholars’ two opinions. If he replaces it with something better while it remains useful, the matter is disputed. And Allah knows best.”

وَسُئِلَ أَيْضًا:
عَنْ وَقْفِ كُلِّ جَمَاعَةٍ تُوُفِّيَ بَعْضُهُمْ وَلَهُ شَقِيقٌ وَوَلَدٌ وَلِلْعُلَمَاءِ فِي ذَلِكَ خِلَافٌ مُسْتَفِيضٌ فِي مَثَلِهِ:
 هَلْ يَخُصُّ الْوَلَدَ أَمْ الْأَخَ؟ فَشَهِدَ قَوْمٌ أَنَّهُ يَخُصُّ الْوَلَدَ دُونَ الْأَخِ بِمُقْتَضَى شَرْطِ الْوَاقِفِ مَعَ عَدَمِ تَحْقِيقِهِمْ الْحَدَّ الْمَوْقُوفَ؛
 بِحَيْثُ إنَّهُمْ غَيَّرُوا بَعْضَ الْحُدُودِ عَمَّا هِيَ عَلَيْهِ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهُمْ ذَلِكَ؟ وَهَلْ لِلْحَاكِمِ أَنْ يَحْكُمَ
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A village has several mosques, some of which have fallen into ruin. Prayer is held in only one of them, and an endowment supports them all. Must the ruined mosques be restored and congregational prayer established in a second mosque? Is it permissible to close them?”

He replied:

“Yes, the mosque must be restored so that prayer can be held in it. Likewise, an imam must be appointed to another mosque when there is a benefit and a need for doing so. It is impermissible to close mosques to the purposes for which they were instituted. However, when the local population is small and one mosque suffices—for example, when they live around it—they are not required to divide their congregation among other mosques.”

He was also asked:

“Regarding the endowment of any group in which a member has died leaving a full brother and a child—scholars differ widely over cases of this kind—does his share go exclusively to the child or to the brother? Some people testified that, under the donor’s stipulation, it belongs exclusively to the child, not the brother, although they had not accurately ascertained the boundaries of the endowed property; indeed, they described some of its boundaries differently from what they actually are. Is it permissible for them to do this? And may the judge rule

الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، الشَّهَادَةُ فِي الْوَقْفِ بِالِاسْتِحْقَاقِ غَيْرُ مَقْبُولَةٍ وَكَذَلِكَ فِي الْإِرْثِ مِنْ الْأُمُورِ الِاجْتِهَادِيَّةِ كَطَهَارَةِ الْمَاءِ وَنَجَاسَتِهِ وَلَكِنْ الشَّاهِدُ يَشْهَدُ بِمَا يَعْلَمُهُ مِنْ الشُّرُوطِ؛ ثُمَّ الْحَاكِمُ يَحْكُمُ فِي الشَّرْطِ بِمُوجِبِ اجْتِهَادِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.

عَنْ وَقَفَ عَلَى رَجُلٍ؛ ثُمَّ عَلَى أَوْلَادِهِ فَاقْتَسَمَهُ الْفَلَّاحُونَ ثُمَّ تَنَاقَلَ بَعْضُهُمْ حِصَّتَهُ إلَى جَانِبِ حِصَّةِ شَرِيكِهِ فَهَلْ تَنْفَسِخُ الْقِسْمَةُ وَالْمُنَاقَلَةُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
لَا تَصِحُّ قِسْمَةُ رَقَبَةِ الْوَقْفِ الْمَوْقُوفِ عَلَى جِهَةٍ وَاحِدَةٍ؛ لَكِنْ تَصِحُّ قِسْمَةُ الْمَنَافِعِ وَهِيَ 
" الْمُهَايَأَةُ "
. وَإِذَا كَانَتْ مُطْلَقَةً لَمْ تَكُنْ لَازِمَةً؛ لَا سِيَّمَا إذَا تَغَيَّرَ الْمَوْقُوفُ فَتَجُوزُ بِغَيْرِ هَذِهِ الْمُهَايَأَةِ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ بَيْعَةٍ بِقَرْيَةِ وَلَهَا وَقْفٌ وَانْقَرَضَ النَّصَارَى بِتِلْكَ الْقَرْيَةِ وَأَسْلَمَ مَنْ بَقِيَ مِنْهُمْ. فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَنْ يُتَّخَذَ مَسْجِدًا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ إذَا لَمْ يَبْقَ مِنْ أَهْلِ الذِّمَّةِ الَّذِينَ اسْتَحَقُّوا تِلْكَ أَحَدٌ جَازَ أَنْ يُتَّخَذَ مَسْجِدًا؛ لَا سِيَّمَا إنْ كَانَتْ بِبَرِّ الشَّامِ فَإِنَّهُ فَتْحُ عَنْوَةٍ.
translated_text:

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah. Testimony asserting entitlement under an endowment is inadmissible; the same applies to inheritance. These are matters requiring independent juristic judgment, like determining whether water is pure or impure. Rather, a witness testifies to the stipulations he knows, and the judge then rules on those stipulations according to his own juristic judgment. Allah knows best.”

He was asked:

“An endowment was established for a man and then for his children. The farmers divided it among themselves, after which some exchanged their portions for ones adjoining their partners’ portions. Are the division and exchanges thereby annulled?”

He replied:

“The underlying property of an endowment dedicated to a single class of beneficiaries cannot validly be partitioned. Its benefits, however, may validly be apportioned; this is called ‘apportionment of use.’ If such an arrangement is unrestricted, it is not binding, especially if the endowed property changes. A different arrangement for apportioning its use may therefore be adopted.”

He was asked:

“A church in a village has an endowment. The Christian community in that village has died out, and those who remained have embraced Islam. May it be made into a mosque?”

He replied:

“Yes. If none of the protected non-Muslims entitled to that church remain, it may be made into a mosque, especially if it is in the territory of Greater Syria, for that territory was conquered by force.”

 بَلْ قَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{لَا قِبْلَتَانِ بِأَرْضِ وَلَا جِزْيَةٍ عَلَى مُسْلِمٍ}
 وَإِذَا كَانَتْ هَذِهِ فِي أَرْضٍ فُتِحَتْ عَنْوَةً وَجَبَ أَنْ تُزَالَ وَلَا تُتْرَكَ مُجَاوِرَةً. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ مَسْجِدٍ لَيْسَ لَهُ وَقْفٌ وَبِجِوَارِهِ سَاحَةٌ:

يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ وَالْحَالَة هَذِهِ؛ فَإِنَّ السَّاحَةَ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ الْمَسْجِدِ؛ كَمَا ذَكَرَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A mosque stands beside a closed, dilapidated church. Some of its walls have fallen onto the mosque’s entrance and the open areas through which it is approached. Part of the wall that collapsed and fell against the mosque’s wall has shifted, and there is fear that its collapse may harm Muslims and those praying in the mosque. If the entire church falls into ruin, may it be demolished?”

He replied:

“Yes. If there is fear of damage to the mosque and harm to those praying in it, whatever threatens the mosque and its worshippers must be removed. If the danger can only be removed by demolition, the church is to be demolished. Indeed, it is established that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

‘Two qiblahs must not coexist in one land, nor may jizyah be imposed on a Muslim.’

“If this church stands in land conquered by force, it must be removed and not left standing beside the mosque. Allah knows best.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A mosque has no endowment, and beside it is an open space. May accommodation for the imam be built there? Please give us a ruling.”

He replied:

“That is permissible in these circumstances, since the open space is not part of the mosque, as stated in the question. Allah knows best.”

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man at a mosque lives off its endowment but does not attend to its needs. The founder of the endowment has children who are in need. May they replace him with someone else and take whatever exceeds the mosque’s needs?”

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah. If he does not fulfil his duties, whoever has the authority to replace him should appoint someone who will fulfil them, unless the first man repents and commits himself to fulfilling his duties. Any surplus beyond the mosque’s needs may be spent on other mosques and on relatives of the endowment’s founder and neighbours of the mosque who are eligible for charity.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“Is it permissible to use the endowment’s income to build accommodation outside the mosque to house those who attend to its needs?”

He replied:

“Yes, they may use the endowment’s income to build accommodation outside the mosque that serves the interests of those entitled to that income who attend to the mosque’s needs.”

وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ مَسْجِدٍ أَعْلَاهُ طَبَقَةٌ وَهُوَ عَتِيقُ الْبِنَاءِ وَأَنَّ الطَّبَقَةَ لَمْ يَسْكُنْهَا أَحَدٌ وَلَمْ يَنْتَفِعْ بِهَا لِكَوْنِهَا سَاقِطَةً وَأَنَّهَا ضَرَرٌ عَلَى الْمَسْجِدِ لِثِقَلِهَا عَلَيْهِ تُخَرِّبُهُ وَلَا لَهُ شَيْءٌ يَعْمُرُ مِنْهُ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ نَقْضُ الطَّبَقَةِ الَّتِي أَعْلَاهُ أَوْ يُغْلَقُ ذَلِكَ الْمَسْجِدُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا كَانَ نَقْضُ الطَّبَقَةِ مَصْلَحَةً لِلْمَسْجِدِ فَتُنْقَضُ وَتُصْرَفُ الْأَنْقَاضُ فِي مَصَالِحِ الْمَسْجِدِ وَإِنْ أَمْكَنَ أَنْ يَشْتَرِيَ بِهَا مَا يُوقِفُ عَلَيْهِ أَوْ يَصْرِفُ فِي عِمَارَتِهِ أَوْ عِمَارَةِ وَقْفِهِ:
 فَعَلَ ذَلِكَ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ اسْتَأْجَرَ أَرْضًا مَوْقُوفَةً وَبَنَى عَلَيْهَا مَا أَرَادَ؛ ثُمَّ أَوْقَفَ ذَلِكَ الْبِنَاءَ وَشَرَطَ أَنْ يُعْطَى الْأُجْرَةَ الْمَوْقُوفَةَ مِنْ رِيعِ وَقْفِهِ عَلَيْهَا وَحَكَمَ الْحَاكِمُ بِصِحَّةِ الْوَقْفِ عَلَى الشُّرُوطِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ فِي الْوَقْفِ. فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ نَقْضٌ ذَلِكَ أَمْ لَا؟
 وَإِذَا أَرَادَ الْوَاقِفُ نَقْضَ الْوَقْفِ بَعْدَ ثُبُوتِهِ لِيُدْخِلَ فِيهِ عَدَدًا آخَرَ بِوَقْفِ ثَانٍ:
 هَلْ يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا حَكَمَ الْحَاكِمُ بِصِحَّةِ الْوَقْفِ لَمْ يَجُزْ فِيهِ تَغْيِيرُهُ وَلَا تَبْدِيلُ شُرُوطِهِ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A mosque is an old building with an upper storey. No one has lived in or benefited from that storey because it is dilapidated. Its weight is damaging the mosque and causing it to deteriorate, and the mosque has no funds for repairs. Is it permissible to dismantle the upper storey, or should the mosque be closed?”

He replied:

“If dismantling the upper storey serves the mosque’s interests, it should be dismantled, and the salvaged materials should be used for the mosque’s benefit. If possible, they should be used to purchase property to be endowed for the mosque, or to fund repairs to the mosque or its endowed property.”

He was asked:

“A man leased endowed land and built upon it as he wished. He then endowed that building, stipulating that the rent for the endowed land be paid from the income of the endowment he had established upon it. The judge ruled that the endowment was valid under the conditions stated in its deed. Is it permissible to revoke it or not?

“If, after the endowment has been legally established, its founder wishes to revoke it in order to include others through a second endowment, is that permissible?”

He replied:

“Once the judge has ruled that the endowment is valid, it may not be altered, nor may its conditions be changed.”

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ وَقْفٍ عَلَى الْفُقَرَاءِ وَالْمَسَاكِينِ وَفِيهِ أَشْجَارُ زَيْتُونٍ وَغَيْرِهِ يَحْمِلُ بَعْضَ السِّنِينَ بِثَمَرِ قَلِيلٍ؛
 فَإِذَا قُطِعَتْ وَبِيعَتْ يُشْتَرَى بِثَمَنِهَا مِلْكٌ يُغَلُّ بِأَكْثَرَ مِنْهَا:
 فَهَلْ لِلنَّاظِرِ ذَلِكَ؟ وَهَلْ إذَا طَالَبَهُ بَعْضُ الْمُسْتَحِقِّينَ لِلْوَقْفِ يَقْطَعُ الشَّجَرَ وَيَبِيعُهُ وَيُقَسِّمُ مِنْهُ عَلَيْهِمْ فَهَلْ لَهُمْ ذَلِكَ؟ أَمْ شِرَاءُ الْمِلْكِ؟
 وَإِذَا تَوَلَّى شَخْصٌ فَوَجَدَ مَنْ تَقَدَّمَهُ غَيَّرَ شَرْطَ الْوَاقِفِ فَجَهَدَ فِي عَمَلِ شَرْطِ الْوَاقِفِ:
 فَهَلْ لَهُ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ مَا جَرَتْ بِهِ الْعَادَةُ مِنْ الجامكية؛
 بِكَوْنِهِ لَمْ يَقْدِرْ أَنْ يَعْمَلَ بِمَا شَرَطَهُ الْوَاقِفُ وَهَذَا النَّاظِرُ فَقِيرٌ لَا مَالَ لَهُ:
 فَهَلْ لَهُ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ مِنْ نِسْبَةِ الْفُقَرَاءِ وَيَكُونُ نَظْرُهُ تَبَرُّعًا بَيِّنُوا لَنَا ذَلِكَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، نَعَمْ يَجُوزُ بَيْعُ تِلْكَ الْأَشْجَارِ وَأَنْ يُشْتَرَى بِهَا مَا يَكُونُ مُغَلُّهُ أَكْثَرَ؛ فَإِنَّ الشَّجَرَ كَالْبِنَاءِ وَلِلنَّاظِرِ أَنْ يُغَيِّرَ صُورَةَ الْوَقْفِ مِنْ صُورَةٍ إلَى صُورَةٍ أَصْلَحَ مِنْهَا كَمَا غَيَّرَ الْخُلَفَاءُ الرَّاشِدُونَ صُورَةَ الْمَسْجِدَيْنِ اللَّذَيْنِ بِالْحَرَمَيْنِ الشَّرِيفَيْنِ وَكَمَا نَقَلَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ مَسْجِدَ الْكُوفَةِ مِنْ مَوْضِعٍ إلَى مَوْضِعٍ وَأَمْثَالِ ذَلِكَ. وَلَا يُقَسَّمُ ثَمَنُ الشَّجَرِ بَيْنَ الْمَوْجُودِينَ؛ لِأَنَّ الشَّجَرَ كَالْبِنَاءِ لَا يَخْتَصُّ بِثَمَنِهِ الْمَوْجُودُونَ؛ وَلَيْسَ هُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الشَّجَرِ وَالزَّرْعِ وَالْمَنَافِعِ الَّتِي يَخْتَصُّ كُلُّ أَهْلِ طَبَقَةٍ بِمَا يُؤْخَذُ فِي زَمَنِهَا مِنْهَا
translated_text:
He was asked:

“An endowment for the poor and needy contains olive trees and other trees that bear little fruit in some years. If they were cut down and sold, their proceeds could purchase property yielding more income. May the administrator do this? If some beneficiaries ask him to cut down the trees, sell them and distribute the proceeds among them, are they entitled to this, or should property be purchased instead?

“If someone assumes responsibility for the endowment and finds that his predecessor has altered the founder’s stipulations, then strives to implement those stipulations, may he receive the customary stipend despite having been unable to fulfil them? This administrator is poor and has no wealth. May he receive something from the share allocated to the poor and administer the endowment without remuneration? Please clarify this for us.”

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah. Yes, those trees may be sold and their proceeds used to purchase something yielding more income. Trees are like buildings: the administrator may change the form of an endowment to one that better serves its interests, just as the Rightly Guided Caliphs altered the form of the two mosques in the two Holy Sanctuaries, and as ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb moved the mosque of Kufa from one location to another, and in other similar cases.

“The proceeds from selling the trees must not be distributed among the current beneficiaries, because trees are like buildings: their sale proceeds do not belong exclusively to the current beneficiaries. This is not on the same footing as trees, crops and benefits from which each successive group of beneficiaries is exclusively entitled to whatever is obtained during its own time.

original_text:
وَأَمَّا النَّاظِرُ فَعَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَعْمَلَ مَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَيْهِ مِنْ الْعَمَلِ الْوَاجِبِ وَيَأْخُذُ لِذَلِكَ الْعَمَلِ مَا يُقَابِلُهُ فَإِنْ كَانَ الْوَاجِبُ عَشَرَةَ أَجْزَاءٍ مِنْ الْعِوَضِ الْمُسْتَحَقِّ أَخَذَهُ وَإِنْ كَانَ يَسْتَحِقُّ الْجَمِيعَ عَلَى مَا يَعْمَلُهُ أَخَذَ الْجَمِيعَ. وَلَهُ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ عَلَى فَقْرِهِ مَا يَأْخُذُهُ الْفَقِيرُ عَلَى فَقْرِهِ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ تَغْيِيرِ صُورَةِ الْوَقْفِ
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 أَمَّا مَا خَرَجَ مِنْ ذَلِكَ عَنْ حُدُودِ الْوَقْفِ إلَى طَرِيقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ وَإِلَى حُقُوقِ الْجِيرَانِ:
 فَيَجِبُ إزَالَتُهُ بِلَا رَيْبٍ. وَأَمَّا مَا خَرَجَ إلَى الطَّرِيقِ النَّافِذِ فَلَا بُدَّ مِنْ إزَالَتِهِ وَأَمَّا إنْ كَانَ خَرَجَ إلَى مِلْكِ الْغَيْرِ فَإِنْ أَذِنَ فِيهِ وَإِلَّا أُزِيلَ. وَأَمَّا تَغْيِيرُ صُورَةِ الْبِنَاءِ مِنْ غَيْرِ عُدْوَانٍ فَيُنْظَرُ فِي ذَلِكَ إلَى الْمَصْلَحَةِ فَإِنْ كَانَتْ هَذِهِ الصُّورَةُ أَصْلَحَ لِلْوَقْفِ وَأَهْلِهِ أُقِرَّتْ. وَإِنْ كَانَ إعَادَتُهَا إلَى مَا كَانَتْ عَلَيْهِ أَصْلَحَ أُعِيدَتْ. وَإِنْ كَانَ بِنَاءُ ذَلِكَ عَلَى صُورَةٍ ثَالِثَةٍ أَصْلَحَ لِلْوَقْفِ بُنِيَتْ. فَيَتْبَعُ فِي صُورَةِ الْبِنَاءِ مَصْلَحَةَ الْوَقْفِ وَيُدَارُ مَعَ الْمَصْلَحَةِ حَيْثُ كَانَتْ. وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ الْخُلَفَاءِ الرَّاشِدِينَ - كَعُمَرِ وَعُثْمَانَ - أَنَّهُمَا قَدْ غَيَّرَا صُورَةَ الْوَقْفِ لِلْمَصْلَحَةِ بَلْ فَعَلَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الْخَطَّابِ مَا هُوَ أَبْلَغُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ حَيْثُ حَوَّلَ مَسْجِدَ الْكُوفَةِ الْقَدِيمِ فَصَارَ سُوقَ التَّمَارِينِ وَبَنَى لَهُمْ مَسْجِدًا فِي مَكَانٍ آخَرَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
As for the administrator, he must perform as much of his obligatory work as he can, and receive remuneration corresponding to that work. If the amount due is ten shares of the remuneration payable, he may take it; and if the work he performs entitles him to the full amount, he may take it all. He may also receive, on account of his poverty, what a poor person receives on that account. Allah knows best.”

He was asked about altering the form of an endowment.

He replied:

“Praise be to Allah. Whatever extends beyond the boundaries of the endowment into the Muslims’ roadway or infringes upon neighbours’ rights must undoubtedly be removed. Whatever extends into a public thoroughfare must be removed. If it extends onto someone else’s property, it may remain with the owner’s permission; otherwise, it must be removed.

“As for altering the form of the building without encroaching upon anyone’s rights, the deciding consideration is the interest served. If its present form better serves the endowment and its beneficiaries, it should be retained. If restoring its former form would serve them better, it should be restored. If rebuilding it in a third form would better serve the endowment, it should be built accordingly. Thus, the form of the building should be determined by the interests of the endowment, adapting to those interests wherever they lie.

“It is established that the Rightly Guided Caliphs, such as ʿUmar and ʿUthmān, altered the form of endowments to serve their interests. Indeed, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb went further than this: he relocated the old mosque of Kufa, whose former site became the date-sellers’ market, and built a mosque for the people elsewhere. Allah knows best.”

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ نَاصَبَ عَلَى أَرْضِ وَقْفٍ عَلَى أَنَّ لِلْوَقْفِ ثُلُثَيْ الشَّجَرِ الْمَنْصُوبِ وَلِلْعَامِلِ الثُّلُثُ:
 فَهَلْ لِمَنْ بَعْدَهُ مِنْ النُّظَّارِ بَيْعُ نَصِيبِ الْوَقْفِ مِنْ الشَّجَرِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
لَا يَجُوزُ لَهُ بَيْعُ ذَلِكَ إلَّا لِحَاجَةِ تَقْتَضِي ذَلِكَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ وَقَفَتْ عَلَى وَلَدَيْهَا دَكَاكِينَ وَدَارًا ثُمَّ بَعْدَ بَنِيهَا وَبَنِيَّ أَوْلَادِهَا يَرْجِعُ عَلَى وَقْفِ مَدْرَسَةِ نُورِ الدِّينِ الشَّهِيدِ وَغَيْرِهِ مِنْ الْمَصَارِفِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ ثُمَّ إنَّ بَعْضَ قَرَائِبِ الْمَرْأَةِ تَعَدَّى وَتَحَيَّلَ وَبَاعَ الْوَقْفَ ثُمَّ إنَّ الْوَرَثَةَ حَاكَمُوا الْمُشْتَرِيَ وَرَقَّمَ الْقَاضِي عَلَى شُهُودِ الْكِتَابِ:
 وَهُوَ صَحِيحٌ ثَابِتٌ. فَقَامَ الْمُشْتَرِي وَأَوْقَفَهَا صَدَقَةً عَلَى خُبْزٍ يُصْرَفُ لِلْمَسَاكِينِ.
 وَجَعَلَ الرَّئِيسُ نَاظِرًا عَلَى الصَّدَقَةِ:
 فَهَلْ يَصِحُّ ذَلِكَ.
 وَإِذَا عَلِمَ الرَّئِيسُ الْعَالِمُ الْمُتَعَبِّدُ أَنَّ هَذَا مُغْتَصِبٌ:
 فَهَلْ يَحِلُّ لَهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ نَاظِرًا عَلَيْهِ وَمَا يَكُونُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
بَيْعُ الْوَقْفِ الصَّحِيحِ اللَّازِمِ الَّذِي يَحْصُلُ بِهِ مَقْصُودُ الْوَقْفِ مِنْ الِانْتِفَاعِ لَا يَجُوزُ وَلَا يَصِحُّ وَقْفُ الْمُشْتَرِي لَهُ وَلَا يَجُوزُ لِلنَّاظِرِ عَلَى الْوَقْفِ الثَّانِي أَنْ يَصْرِفَهُ إلَى غَيْرِ الْمُسْتَحِقِّينَ قَبْلُ وَلَا يَتَصَرَّفَ فِيهِ بِغَيْرِ مُسَوِّغٍ شَرْعِيٍّ سَوَاءٌ تَصَرَّفَ بِحُكْمِ النَّظْرِ الْبَاطِلِ أَوْ بِغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
translated_text:
He was asked:

Someone entered into a tree-planting arrangement on endowed land, stipulating that the endowment would receive two-thirds of the trees planted and the worker one-third. May succeeding administrators sell the endowment’s share of the trees?

He replied:

“He may not sell it unless a need requires this. Allah knows best.”

He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A woman endowed shops and a house for her two children, stipulating that, after her sons and her children’s sons, the endowment should revert to the endowment of the school of Nūr al-Dīn al-Shahīd and other purposes sanctioned by Islamic law. Some of the woman’s relatives then wrongfully and fraudulently sold the endowed property. The heirs brought proceedings against the purchaser, and the judge entered an annotation concerning the witnesses to the deed, which was valid and duly established. The purchaser then made the property a charitable endowment to provide bread for the poor, with the chief appointed as its administrator. Is this valid? If the chief, a learned and devout man, knows that this person has wrongfully seized the property, is it lawful for him to serve as its administrator? What is the ruling?

He replied:

“It is not permissible to sell property belonging to a valid, binding endowment that continues to provide its intended benefit. Nor is the purchaser’s endowment of it valid. The administrator of the second endowment may not direct its benefits to anyone other than the original beneficiaries, or deal with it without a justification sanctioned by Islamic law, whether he acts under that invalid administrative appointment or otherwise. Allah knows best.”

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ بَنَى حَائِطًا فِي مَقْبَرَةِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ؛
 يَقْصِدُ أَنْ يَحُوزَ نَفْعَهُ لِدَفْنِ مَوْتَاهُ فَادَّعَى رَجُلٌ أَنَّ لَهُ مَوْتَى تَحْتَ الْحَائِطِ وَمَا هُوَ دَاخِلَ الْحَائِطِ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ لَهُ ذَلِكَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:

A man built a wall in a Muslim cemetery, intending to reserve the enclosed area for burying his own dead. Another man claimed that some of his dead lay beneath the wall and within the enclosure. Is he permitted to do this?

He replied:

“He has no right to build a wall in a Muslim cemetery or to reserve any part of it exclusively for himself, to the exclusion of others entitled to use it. Allah knows best.”

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A public water conduit has an overflow that discharges into a wastewater channel. Nearby is a conduit carrying pure water, but its supply is small. Is it permissible to divert that overflow to the ablution facility? Will the person who does this be rewarded? Is it permissible to prevent him from doing so?

He replied:

“Yes, this is permissible with the ruler’s permission. It is not permissible to prevent it if preventing it serves no interest recognized by Islamic law. Whoever works to bring this about will be rewarded. Allah knows best.”

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked: (*)

About an endowment for which compensation is used to purchase something to take its place. An example is an endowment destroyed by someone: compensation is collected from him and used to purchase its replacement. Scholars unanimously agree that anyone who destroys an endowment is liable to compensate for it. Liability also arises from possession. Thus, if someone unlawfully seizes it and it perishes while in his wrongful possession, he must compensate for it, by scholarly agreement. Some scholars have, however, disagreed over whether unlawful seizure entails liability for certain kinds of property, such as real estate, and whether certain kinds, such as movable property, may validly be endowed. Nevertheless, they have not disputed that compensation is due for its destruction at someone’s hands, as with other property.

This differs from the case of a slave woman who has borne her master a child. Although scholars agree that compensation is due for causing her death, they disagree over whether liability also arises from possession of her. Most—including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad—hold that it does. Abū Hanīfa, however, holds that it does not.

Liability arising from possession is contractual liability, such as the seller’s responsibility to deliver the item sold, to ensure that it is free of defects, and to ensure that it was rightfully sold. His liability for recourse arising from the sale follows from the contract, even if he has not expressly stipulated it.

One of the established grounds for purchasing a replacement with the proceeds of an endowment is that the endowment has ceased to provide any benefit. In that case, according to the school of Ahmad and others, it is sold and its price used to purchase something to take its place. May it be exchanged for something better while it is still producing income? There are two opinions within his school. Permitting this is the position of Abū Thawr and others.

This is not a question addressed to the shaykh, but rather a statement by him—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—as is evident. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
The point is this: where replacement is permissible, must the replacement be on the same street or in the same town as the original endowment? Or may it be elsewhere if that would better serve the endowment’s beneficiaries—for example, if they reside in a different town and purchasing the replacement there would benefit them more through greater income and easier access?

We say: I know of no one who has stipulated that the replacement must be in the town of the original endowment. Rather, Ahmad’s explicit statements and principles, together with the general and unrestricted wording of his statements and those of his followers, entail doing whatever best serves the endowment’s beneficiaries. His guiding principle in this matter is to safeguard the interests of the endowment. Indeed, his guiding principle regarding contracts generally is to consider people’s interests. Allah has commanded righteousness and forbidden corruption, and has sent His messengers to secure and perfect benefits and to eliminate and reduce harms.

“And Moses said to his brother Aaron, ‘Take my place among my people, put things right, and do not follow the way of those who spread corruption.’”

Shuayb said:

“I only intend reform as far as I am able.”

And the Most High said:

“Whoever fears Allah and sets things right—no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.”

And the Most High said:

“When it is said to them, ‘Do not spread corruption on earth,’ they say, ‘We are only reformers.’”

“Indeed, it is they who spread corruption.”

Ahmad ibn Hanbal permitted replacing one mosque with another when this served a beneficial purpose, just as he permitted alterations to a mosque for such a purpose. He cited as evidence that Umar ibn al-Khattāb—may Allah be pleased with him—replaced the old mosque of Kufa with another mosque, and the first mosque became a market for date sellers.

Ahmad also permitted relocating a mosque to another village if its locality fell into ruin. Indeed, according to the stronger of the two opinions reported from him, that mosque may be sold and its price used to build another mosque in a different village if it is no longer needed in the first village.  وَإِنْ كَانَ الْفَرَسُ حَبِيسًا عَلَى جَمِيعِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ فَهُوَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْوَقْفِ عَلَى جِهَةٍ عَامَّةٍ:
 كَالْمَسَاجِدِ وَالْوَقْفِ عَلَى الْمَسَاكِينِ.
 وَمِمَّا يُبَيِّنُ هَذَا:

 هَلْ يَشْتَرِي بِهِ مَا يَقُومُ مَقَامَهُ إذَا كَانَ الْعِوَضُ مَنْقُولًا؟ فَأَنْ يَشْتَرِيَ بِهَذَا الْعِوَضِ فِي بَلَدِ مُقَامِهِمْ أَوْلَى مِنْ أَنْ يَشْتَرِيَ بِهِ فِي مَكَانِ الْعَقَارِ الْأَوَّلِ إذَا كَانَ ذَلِكَ أَصْلَحَ لَهُمْ؛ إذْ لَيْسَ فِي تَخْصِيصِ مَكَانِ الْعَقَارِ
translated_text:
a village other than the original one. Since mosques are shared by all Muslims, there is even stronger justification for relocating an endowment dedicated to particular people to their town than there is for relocating a mosque. An endowment for specified beneficiaries is their exclusive right, in which no one else shares. At most, after their line has died out, it may pass to a general charitable cause, such as the poor and needy; it would then be like a mosque.

Thus, if having the endowment in their town would benefit them more, purchasing its replacement there is what its administrator ought to do. This is comparable to an endowed horse that is sold and replaced with something purchased for its value: if it was endowed for people at one frontier post who subsequently moved to another, purchasing the replacement at the frontier post where the horse is secured takes precedence over purchasing it at another post. If, however, the horse is endowed for all Muslims, it is like an endowment for a general charitable cause, such as mosques or endowments for the needy.

This is further illustrated by the following: if the endowed property were movable—such as lighting, weapons, or scholarly books—and were endowed for the specified descendants of a man, it could be kept wherever they lived. Indeed, that would be the required course, unlike an endowment dedicated to the inhabitants of a particular town.

But if compensation is obtained for it, should that compensation, when movable, be used to purchase something to take its place? Purchasing the replacement with this compensation in the town where the beneficiaries reside takes precedence over purchasing it at the location of the original real estate, if that would benefit them more; for specifying the location of the property

Thus, someone purchasing a replacement with the compensation is neither obliged nor recommended to retain the original location. Rather, choosing another location is permissible. It may be recommended, and may even be obligatory when the benefit can only be secured by doing so. And Allah knows best.

translated_text:
Chapter on Gifts and Donations

Shaykh al-Islām—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

Which is better: charity or a gift?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. “Charity” is what is given for Allah’s sake as a pure act of worship, without any particular regard for a specific individual or seeking anything from him. Rather, it is directed to appropriate recipients of charity, such as those in need.

A “gift,” however, is intended to honor a particular person, whether out of love, friendship, or a desire to have a need fulfilled. For this reason, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, would accept gifts and reciprocate them, so that no one would have a favor to hold over him. He would not consume the impurities people shed to cleanse themselves of their sins—namely, charitable offerings. For this and other reasons, he would not partake of charity.

Once this distinction is clear, charity is better, unless a gift serves a purpose that makes it better than charity. Examples include giving a gift to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, during his lifetime out of love for him; giving a gift to a relative to maintain ties of kinship; and giving to a brother for Allah’s sake. Such giving may be better than charity.

translated_text:
He was also asked:

If someone gives another man a gift of something whose particulars are unknown, or grants him permission to use it, is this valid? For example, what if he allows him to take the fruit of a tree next year? And if he wishes to revoke this, may he validly do so?

He replied:

The scholars have differed over giving gifts whose particulars are unknown. Mālik permitted this, even allowing someone to give another whatever he had inherited from a certain person, without knowing its amount or whether it was a third or a quarter. The same applies if he gives him a share of a house without knowing how large that share is. He likewise permits giving something not yet in existence, such as the fruit of one’s trees for the current year or for ten years. Al-Shāfiʿī did not permit this. The recognized position in the schools of Abū Hanīfah and Ahmad is likewise to prohibit it. However, Ahmad and others permit forms of settlement concerning undetermined claims, and release from such claims, that al-Shāfiʿī does not permit. Abū Hanīfah likewise permits some such arrangements that al-Shāfiʿī does not.

Al-Shāfiʿī requires the amount of the subject matter to be known in most contracts, even the compensation for a wife’s release from marriage, the dower, and the terms stipulated for non-Muslims under Muslim protection. Most scholars allow greater latitude in this regard. This is discussed in its proper place. Mālik’s position on this issue is stronger.

This question is connected to another fundamental principle: contracts of exchange, such as sale, marriage, and compensated divorce, become binding before possession is taken. Thus, taking possession—which follows from and is entailed by the contract—

There is disagreement within Ahmad’s school, as there is concerning specifically identified property: does the contract alone make it binding, or must possession be taken? Two opinions are reported from him. The same applies to certain forms of loans for use. The early generations regularly lent trees for their produce and livestock for their milk. Likewise, they gave gifts of fruit and milk not yet produced, regarding these arrangements as binding. This, however, resembles a loan for use, because the subject of the contract comes into being gradually, like the benefit derived from an asset. Hence such produce, like the benefits of an endowment, is among the things to which its beneficiary is entitled. Accordingly, arrangements involving remuneration with a share of such produce are valid, such as tending trees for a share of their fruit.

As for granting permission to use such things, the scholars do not dispute its permissibility, whether the thing concerned already exists or has yet to exist, and whether its particulars are known or unknown. Such permission, however, does not constitute a binding contract, just as a loan for use is not binding according to those who hold that view, such as Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfiʿī. Mālik, by contrast, regards it as binding when its limits are defined by stipulation or custom. Within Ahmad’s school there are differing views and further distinctions.

He—may Allah have mercy on him—was also asked:

A woman gave her husband her document. She had no father, but did have brothers. Are they entitled to prevent her from doing this?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah, Lord of all worlds. Her brothers have neither guardianship over her nor authority to restrict her disposal of her property. If she is legally competent to give away her property, her gift is valid whether they approve or not. Allah knows best.

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A woman had children by different fathers. She singled out one child and gave him a share of her property as a charitable gift, to the exclusion of his siblings. She then died while still residing in the property she had given away. Is the charitable gift valid or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. If he had not taken possession of it before she died, the gift became void according to the well-known position in the schools of the four imams. If she had delivered it into his possession, then, according to the correct view, the recipient may not retain it exclusively; rather, it must be shared between him and his siblings. Allah knows best.

He also said:

Section

As for contracts whose binding and settled status depends on taking possession—such as charitable gifts, gifts, pledges, and endowments, according to those who hold that taking possession is a condition for the contract to become binding—these too are valid for undivided shares according to the majority of scholars, including Mālik, al-Shāfiʿī, and Ahmad. Abū Hanīfah did not permit them, arguing that taking possession is a condition of these contracts, yet possession cannot be taken before partition.

The majority, however, maintain that possession is taken under these contracts just as it is in a sale, even though taking possession is a consequence of a sale, not a condition of its validity or binding force. Possession can also be taken of property that cannot be divided, for they unanimously agree that an undivided share of such property may be given as a gift, since partition is impossible.

Moreover, when someone gives an undivided share whose gift is unanimously held valid—such as a share in indivisible property—or a share whose gift is disputed, according to those who permit it, such as Mālik, al-Shāfi‘ī, and Ahmad, and it is duly taken into possession and held by the recipient of the gift or charitable donation, it thereby becomes binding by the consensus of the Muslims. The recipient may then exercise all rights of disposal permitted in jointly owned property. He may sell it or give it away; alternatively, the donor and the recipient may agree to divide its use by allocating separate areas or periods of time. They may also rent it out together, as co-owners do with the owner of the share that was not given away. If the donor exercises his rights by residing alongside the recipient, whether under an arrangement dividing their use or otherwise, this neither diminishes nor invalidates the gift. Whoever says otherwise has contravened the consensus of the Muslims.

As for the matters set out by the jurists of Mālik’s school in their books—stipulating an option; holding that the property’s remaining in the donor’s possession, whether through rental, borrowing, or otherwise, invalidates the taking of possession; holding that the recipient’s taking possession is invalidated if the property returns to the donor shortly afterwards, while there is disagreement if it returns after a longer period, such as a year; and holding that the gift becomes void if the donor falls ill or becomes insolvent before possession is taken, and similar matters—these all concern the donated property itself.

The same applies to their disagreement over whether the donor may be compelled to deliver possession. According to Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī, he may not be compelled, whereas according to Mālik, he may. Two positions are reported from Ahmad concerning unfair pricing.

All these and similar questions concern the donated property itself, whether separately owned or an undivided share. As for the half that remains in the donor’s ownership, they agree—with an agreement necessarily known among scholars of Islamic law as part of the religion of Islam—that the owner’s exercise of his rights over it does not invalidate the gift or the possession previously taken of the donated share. They also agree that these two co-owners may exercise their rights just as other co-owners do. Any student of jurisprudence who imagines that

after possession of the undivided share has been delivered, the two parties’ living in the house—one occupying the half that remains his and the other occupying the other half, whether under an arrangement dividing their use or otherwise—invalidates the gift, as Mālik holds in the case of residence in the donated property itself, has contravened the consensus of the Muslims. Such a person is far removed from any sound grasp of jurisprudence or knowledge of Islamic law. For if this were correct, someone who gave away an undivided share would be prevented from benefiting from what remained his, and would be in the same position as someone who had given away the whole property.

Moreover, the jurists discussed this only in relation to the donated property, because the donor’s continued control over it, or its return to him shortly afterwards, ordinarily precludes the recipient’s taking possession. This might also become a means of making a gift without transferring possession: the donor could portray his residence there as a loan for use, as a stratagem. Hence it is reported that ‘Uthmān, may Allah be pleased with him, said:

“What is the matter with people who give their children gifts, but if a man’s child dies, he says, ‘It is my property and remains in my possession,’ yet in the event of his own death, his claim is, ‘I had given it to him’? Only what the child has taken into possession from his father’s property is established as a gift.”

They then asked him about a young child, and he said, “His father’s possession counts as possession on his behalf.” Mālik and others adopted this position. This is clear in itself, whether the donated property is separately owned or an undivided share.

As for the other share, which was not given away, it is like a separate item of property that was not given away. Its owner exercises the rights of a co-owner: if the property requires repairs, he is compelled to undertake them according to Ahmad and according to the apparent position of Mālik’s school. The right of pre-emption also applies to it. Where physical division of the property is possible—that is, if it is divisible—it may be divided.

 كَانَ هَذَا بَعِيدًا مِنْ التَّمَيُّزِ فِي الْأَحْكَامِ الشَّرْعِيَّةِ وَالْمَسَائِلِ الْفِقْهِيَّةِ وَلَيْسَتْ هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةُ مِمَّا تَقْبَلُ النِّزَاعَ وَالْخِلَافَ أَصْلًا وَمِنْ الْعَجَبِ أَنَّهُمْ يَطْلُبُونَ النَّقْلَ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَسْأَلَةِ مِنْ 
" كِتَابِ الْهِبَةِ وَالصَّدَقَةِ "
 وَنَحْوِ ذَلِكَ؛ وَلَيْسَ هَذَا مَوْضِعَهَا؛ وَإِنَّمَا مَوْضِعُهَا 
" كِتَابُ الشَّرِكَةِ وَالْقِسْمَةِ "
 وَنَحْوُ ذَلِكَ؛ فَإِنَّ السُّؤَالَ إنَّمَا وَقَعَ عَنْ التَّصَرُّفِ فِي الشِّقْصِ الْبَاقِي لَمْ يَقَعْ فِي النَّصِيبِ الْمَوْهُوبِ وَإِنْ تَخَيَّلَ مُتَخَيِّلٌ أَنَّ التساكت يَقْتَضِي ثُبُوتَ يَدِ كُلٍّ مِنْهُمَا عَلَى الْجَمِيعِ.
 قِيلَ لَهُ:
 فَحِينَئِذٍ تَكُونُ يَدُ كُلٍّ مِنْ الشَّرِيكَيْنِ عَلَى جَمِيعِ الْمُشْتَرَكِ وَإِنْ صَحَّ هَذَا لَمْ يَصِحَّ يَدُ الْمُشْتَرِكِ بِحَالِ فَإِنَّ أَبَا حَنِيفَةَ إنَّمَا قَالَهُ فِيمَا يَقْبَلُ الْقِسْمَةَ ثُمَّ إذَا قُدِّرَ أَنَّ يَدَ الشَّرِيكِ عَلَى الْجَمِيعِ فَهَذِهِ لَا تَمْنَعُ الْحِيَازَةَ الْمُعْتَبَرَةَ فِي الْمَشَاعِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا وَهَبَ شِقْصًا مِنْ عَيْنٍ فَإِنَّمَا عَلَيْهِ أَنْ يَقْبِضَ الْمَوْهُوبَ فَقَطْ مَعَ بَقَاءِ يَدِهِ عَلَى مَا لَمْ يَهَبْهُ؛
 سَوَاءٌ قِيلَ:
 إنَّ بَقَاءَ يَدِهِ عَلَى نَصِيبِهِ يَعُمُّ الْجَمِيعَ أَوْ لَا يَعُمُّ. فَعُلِمَ أَنَّ اسْتِيلَاءَ الشَّرِيكِ الْوَاهِبِ عَلَى نَصِيبِهِ وَتَصَرُّفِهِ فِيهِ لَا يَمْنَعُ الْحَوْزَ ابْتِدَاءً وَلَا يَمْنَعُهُ دَوَامًا بِاتِّفَاقِ الْمُسْلِمِينَ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ وَهَبَ رُبُعَ مَكَانٍ فَتَبَيَّنَ أَقَلُّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ هَلْ تَبْطُلُ الْهِبَةُ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
لَا تَبْطُلُ.
translated_text:
al-Shāfiʿī. This is clear to anyone with even a slight acquaintance with Islamic jurisprudence, provided he understands the jurists’ reasoning. But someone who fails to distinguish between these matters, and imagines that the rulings they mention concerning the donated property apply both to it and to the other share, shows a profound lack of discernment in legal rulings and questions of jurisprudence. This issue admits of no dispute or disagreement whatsoever.

It is astonishing that they seek a transmitted ruling on this issue in the “Book of Gifts and Charity” and similar sections. That is not where it belongs; rather, it belongs in the “Book of Co-ownership and Partition” and similar sections. The question concerns dealings with the remaining share, not with the donated share.

If someone imagines that their tacit acquiescence establishes each party’s possession of the whole, the answer is: in that case, each co-owner would possess the entirety of the jointly owned property. If this argument were sound, a co-owner’s possession could never be valid under any circumstances. Abū Hanīfah stated this only concerning property capable of division.

Moreover, even supposing that a co-owner’s possession extends to the whole, this does not preclude the taking of possession required for an undivided share. When someone gives away a share in a particular property, he need only deliver possession of what he has given, while retaining possession of what he has not given. This holds whether his continued possession of his own share is said to extend to the whole or not. Thus, by the consensus of the Muslims, the donor’s control over his own share and his dealings with it neither prevent possession from being taken initially nor invalidate its continuation.

He was asked:

“Someone gave away a quarter of a property, but it turned out to be less than that. Is the gift invalid?”

He answered:

“It is not invalid.”

translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

“A man had two daughters and a pregnant former wife. He assigned two thousand dinars and four properties to his daughters in writing. His former wife subsequently gave birth to a son, but he assigned nothing to him. The father later died, leaving assets in addition to what he had assigned to his daughters. These remaining assets were divided among them according to the prescribed rules of Islamic inheritance. Should what he assigned to the daughters be revoked or not?”

He answered:

“Scholars disagree on this matter if he had fully transferred ownership to the daughters and possession had been taken.

“But if he merely recorded two thousand dinars as a liability owed by him to them, without delivering possession, or gave them something without taking possession of it on their behalf, then this transaction is revoked, and everything is divided among the son and the two daughters.

“If possession was taken, however, there is disagreement. It is reported that Saʿd ibn ʿUbādah divided his wealth among his children. After his death, a child conceived during his lifetime was born to him, and Abū Bakr and ʿUmar ordered that the child be given his share of the inheritance. The same should therefore be done in this case, for the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

‘Fear Allah and treat your children fairly.’

“He also said to someone who wished to single out some of his children for a gift:

‘I will not bear witness to injustice.’

“The daughters must fear Allah and give the son his due.”

translated_text:
The Prophet’s words—peace and blessings be upon him—to the man who singled out some of his children, “Have someone other than me witness this,” were a warning to him, for he also said:

“Take it back.”

That man did indeed take it back. If, however, he made a bequest to the daughters to take effect after his death, it is not binding, by scholarly consensus. The correct scholarly view is that a man who singles out his daughters for gifts while excluding his unborn child must revoke those gifts during his lifetime, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, commanded. If he dies without revoking them, they must be revoked after his death as well, according to the sounder of the two views, in obedience to Allah and His Messenger, in observance of the justice commanded, and in following the example of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both. The favoured recipient may not lawfully take the excess; rather, that recipient must share all the property with their siblings according to the justice Allah has commanded. Allah, glorified and exalted is He, knows best.

He was asked:

“A man owns a slave woman and permits his son to enjoy intimacy and have intercourse with her, without transferring ownership of her to him, giving her to him as a gift, or doing anything else of that kind. The slave woman then bears a child to her owner’s son. Does permission to enjoy intimacy and have intercourse with her constitute a transfer of ownership to the son? Is the child free, and does the slave woman acquire the status of umm walad (a slave woman who has borne her master a child) in relation to her owner’s son, so that her owner—the young man’s father, who permitted his son to enjoy intimacy and have intercourse with her—is forbidden to sell her?”

translated_text:
through conduct: whatever people regard as a sale, gift, or lease is treated accordingly. The well-known position of al-Shāfiʿī requires a verbal formula, except in certain specified cases. Where a verbal formula is used, however, the majority hold that Islamic law prescribes no fixed wording; rather, whether the wording conveys the transaction is determined by customary usage. This is the position of the majority.

Accordingly, they recognize a gift as valid when expressed in such words as: “I grant you this house for your lifetime,” “I give you this food to eat,” or “I provide you with this animal to ride,” and similar expressions that those addressed understand as conveying a gift. Likewise, providing a woman with her bridal furnishings when she goes to her husband’s home constitutes a transfer of ownership to her, as the jurists of the schools of Abū Hanīfah, Ahmad, and others have ruled. This is because Allah mentions sales, leases, and gifts in His Book in general terms, without a fixed definition in either language or Islamic law; their meaning is therefore determined by custom. The purpose of speech is to convey meanings, so any wording that conveys the intended transaction suffices to conclude the contract.

Accordingly, under people’s customary practice, if someone buys a slave woman for his son and says, “Take her for yourself and enjoy intimacy with her,” or something similar, they regard this as a transfer of ownership.

Furthermore, if someone knows that intercourse with a slave woman is permissible only by virtue of ownership, then, in permitting his son to enjoy intimacy with her, he can only intend to transfer ownership of her to him. Thus, if something has occurred that signifies a transfer of ownership according to the majority of scholars—and theirs is the sounder of the two views—the son has had intercourse with a woman he owns. His child is free, with paternity established as his, and the slave woman becomes his umm walad; she may not be sold, given away, or inherited.

If, however, it is assumed that the father did nothing whatsoever to transfer ownership, but the son believed that he had become her owner, his child is likewise free, with paternity established as his, and he is not liable to the prescribed punishment. And if

Mālik holds that he acquires ownership of her upon payment of her value, whether or not she becomes pregnant. The other three imams hold that he does not thereby acquire ownership of her.

According to Mālik’s view, therefore, she likewise belongs to the son and becomes his umm walad, and his child is free. According to the other three imams, the slave woman does not become his umm walad. But is the child free—as in the case of someone who has intercourse with his wife’s slave woman with her permission? Two positions are reported from Ahmad. The first is that the child is not free; this is also the position of Abū Hanīfah, even if the man believed that she was lawful for him. The second is that the child is free. This is the correct view when the man believed that she was lawful for him. It is the expressly stated position of al-Shāfi'ī and Ahmad concerning a pledgee: if he has intercourse with a slave woman pledged to him, with the pledgor’s permission, believing that this is permissible, his child is free from conception because of the legal doubt involved. Doubt arising from belief or ownership precludes the prescribed punishment by agreement of the imams. It likewise affects the child’s freedom and paternity, just as when someone has intercourse with her under an invalid marriage or invalid ownership: the child is free by agreement of the imams.

Abū Hanīfah disagrees with the two of them in this case and holds that the child is a slave. Mālik, however, holds that the man has acquired ownership of the slave woman through the intercourse for which permission was given.

Must the man who had intercourse with permission pay the child’s value? Al-Shāfi'ī has two views on this. The first, which is also Ahmad’s expressly stated position, is that he is not obliged to pay the child’s value, because he had intercourse with the owner’s permission. He was asked:

A woman, while in sound health, gave her son a charitable gift consisting of a share of everything capable of division, over a period increasing every ten years. The donor then died. During his own lifetime, the recipient subsequently gave his son everything his mother had given him. After the first donor’s death, all of this was established before a judge, who issued a ruling accordingly. May the remaining heirs have this invalidated on the grounds of his continued residence there after it had been handed over to her son, the recipient, or not?

He replied—may Allah have mercy on him:

If this charitable gift remained in the donor’s possession until the donor died, it became void according to the well-known positions of all the imams. If the judge established that the transaction had taken place, his establishing that fact does not entail its validity. As for ruling that it is valid under these circumstances when the donor has heirs, no knowledgeable judge would do so—unless the case is not as described, in which event he would not be ruling on this matter. He was asked:

A man owned a house and gave one-half and one-quarter of it as a charitable gift to his own son, while giving the remaining quarter to his full sister. The son to whom he had given the half and the quarter subsequently died. The donor then gave the entire house as a charitable gift to his daughter. Is this final gift valid, rendering the earlier gifts void, or not?

He replied:

If he had transferred ownership of the quarter to his sister and she had taken possession of it, and had transferred ownership of the three-quarters to his son, then the sister’s property passes to her heirs, not to the daughter. The owner has no right to transfer it to his daughter. And Allah knows best.

عَنْ امْرَأَةٍ مَاتَتْ وَلَهَا أَبٌ وَأُمٌّ وَزَوْجٌ وَهِيَ رَشِيدَةٌ. وَقَدْ أَخَذَ أَبُوهَا الْقُمَاشَ. وَلَمْ يُعْطِ الْوَرَثَةَ شَيْئًا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
لَا يُقْبَلُ مِنْهُ ذَلِكَ؛ بَلْ مَا كَانَ فِي يَدِهَا مِنْ الْمَالِ فَهُوَ لَهَا يَنْتَقِلُ إلَى وَرَثَتِهَا. وَإِنْ كَانَ هُوَ اشْتَرَاهُ وَجَهَّزَهَا بِهِ عَلَى الْوَجْهِ الْمُعْتَادِ فِي الْجَهَازِ فَهُوَ تَمْلِيكٌ لَهَا. فَلَيْسَ لَهُ الرُّجُوعُ بَعْدَ مَوْتِهَا.
وَسُئِلَ:
هَلْ لِمَنْ أُهْدِيَ كَلْبَ صَيْدٍ فَأَهْدَى لِلْمُهْدَى عِوَضًا هَلْ لَهُ أَكْلُ هَذِهِ الْهَدِيَّةَ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا أَعْطَى الْكَلْبَ الْمُعَلَّمَ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ مِنْ نِيَّتِهِ أَنْ يَأْخُذَ عِوَضًا وَلَا قَصْدَ بِالْهَدِيَّةِ الثَّوَابَ؛ بَلْ إكْرَامًا لِلْمُهْدَى إلَيْهِ ثُمَّ إنَّ الْمُهْدَى إلَيْهِ أَعْطَاهُ شَيْئًا فَلَا بَأْسَ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A woman of sound judgment died, leaving a father, a mother, and a husband. Her father took her household effects and gave the heirs nothing. What is the ruling?

He replied:

This cannot be accepted from him. Rather, whatever property was in her possession belonged to her and passes to her heirs. Even if he bought it himself and provided it for her as her bridal trousseau in the customary manner, this constitutes a transfer of ownership to her. He therefore has no right to take it back after her death.

He was asked:

If someone is given a hunting dog and gives the donor a gift in return, may the donor benefit from that gift?

He replied:

If he gave the trained dog without intending to receive anything in exchange or seeking a return for his gift, but simply to honour the recipient, and the recipient subsequently gave him something, there is nothing wrong with that.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى -:
عَمَّا إذَا وَهَبَ لِإِنْسَانِ شَيْئًا ثُمَّ رَجَعَ فِيهِ:
 هَلْ يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 فِي السُّنَنِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ:
 
{لَيْسَ لِوَاهِبِ أَنْ يَرْجِعَ فِي هِبَتِهِ؛ إلَّا الْوَالِدُ فِيمَا وَهَبَهُ لِوَلَدِهِ}
 . وَهَذَا مَذْهَبُ الشَّافِعِيِّ وَمَالِكٌ وَأَحْمَد وَغَيْرِهِمْ؛
 إلَّا أَنْ يَكُونَ الْمَقْصُودُ بِالْهِبَةِ الْمُعَاوَضَةَ:
 مِثْلَ مَنْ يُعْطِي رَجُلًا عَطِيَّةً لِيُعَاوِضَهُ عَلَيْهَا أَوْ يَقْضِيَ لَهُ حَاجَةً: فَهَذَا إذَا لَمْ يُوفِ بِالشَّرْطِ الْمَعْرُوفِ لَفْظًا أَوْ عُرْفًا فَلَهُ أَنْ يَرْجِعَ فِي هِبَتِهِ أَوْ قَدْرِهَا. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ الرَّجُلِ يَهَبُ الرَّجُلَ شَيْئًا:
 إمَّا ابْتِدَاءً؛
 أَوْ يَكُونُ دَيْنًا عَلَيْهِ ثُمَّ يَحْصُلُ بَيْنَهُمَا شَنَآنٌ فَيَرْجِعُ فِي هِبَتِهِ:
 فَهَلْ لَهُ ذَلِكَ؟
 وَإِذَا أَنْكَرَ الْهِبَةَ وَحَلَفَ الْمَوْهُوبُ لَهُ أَنَّهُ لَا يَسْتَحِقُّ الْوَاهِبُ فِي ذِمَّتِهِ شَيْئًا:
 هَلْ يَحْنَثُ أَمْ لَا؟
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

If someone gives another person a gift and then takes it back, is that permissible?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. It is reported in the Sunan collections that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“A donor may not take back his gift, except a father regarding what he has given his child.”

This is the position of al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik, Ahmad and others. An exception applies when the gift is intended to secure something in return: for example, someone gives a man a gift so that he will reciprocate or attend to a need of his. If the recipient does not fulfil the condition established explicitly or by custom, the donor may recover his gift or its equivalent value. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man gives another man something, either as a new gift or by forgiving a debt owed to him. Then hostility arises between them, and he takes back his gift. Is he entitled to do so? If the donor denies having made the gift, and the recipient swears that he owes the donor nothing, does he thereby swear falsely?

original_text:
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، لَيْسَ لِوَاهِبِ أَنْ يَرْجِعَ فِي هِبَتِهِ غَيْرَ الْوَالِدِ؛ إلَّا أَنْ تَكُونَ الْهِبَةُ عَلَى جِهَةِ الْمُعَاوَضَةِ لَفْظًا أَوْ عُرْفًا فَإِذَا كَانَتْ لِأَجْلِ عِوَضٍ وَلَمْ يَحْصُلْ فَلِلْوَاهِبِ الرُّجُوعُ فِيهَا. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَمَّنْ وُهِبَ لِابْنِهِ هِبَةً ثُمَّ تَصَرَّفَ فِيهَا وَادَّعَى أَنَّهَا مِلْكُهُ:
 فَهَلْ يَتَضَمَّنُ هَذَا الرُّجُوعَ فِي الْهِبَةِ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ يَتَضَمَّنُ ذَلِكَ الرُّجُوعَ. وَاَللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ وَهَبَ لِإِنْسَانِ فَرَسًا ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ بِمُدَّةِ طَلَبَ الْوَاهِبُ مِنْهُ أُجْرَتَهَا فَقَالَ لَهُ:
 مَا أَقْدِرُ عَلَى شَيْءٍ؛ وَإِلَّا فَرَسُك خُذْهَا.
 قَالَ الْوَاهِبُ:
 مَا آخُذُهَا إلَّا أَنْ تُعْطِيَنِي أُجْرَتَهَا: فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ ذَلِكَ وَتَجُوزُ لَهُ أُجْرَةٌ أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
إذَا أَعَادَ إلَيْهِ الْعَيْنَ الْمَوْهُوبَةَ فَلَا شَيْءَ لَهُ غَيْرَ ذَلِكَ وَلَيْسَ لَهُ الْمُطَالَبَةُ بِأُجْرَتِهَا وَلَا مُطَالَبَتُهُ بِالضَّمَانِ؛ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ ضَامِنًا لَهَا وَكَانَ يُطْعِمُهَا بِانْتِفَاعِهِ بِهَا مُقَابَلَةً لِذَلِكَ.
translated_text:
He replied:

Praise be to Allah. A donor may not take back his gift, except a father, unless the gift was intended to secure something in return, whether expressly stipulated or understood by custom. If it was given in return for something that was not received, the donor may take it back. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A gift was given to a man’s son, after which the man disposed of it and claimed that it belonged to him. Does this constitute taking back the gift?

He replied:

Yes, this constitutes taking it back. And Allah knows best.

He was asked:

A man gave someone a horse. Some time later, the donor demanded payment for its use. The recipient told him, “I cannot afford to pay anything. If that is not acceptable, take back your horse.” The donor said, “I will not take it back unless you pay me for its use.” Is this permissible, and is he entitled to payment for its use?

He replied:

If the recipient returns the gifted property itself, the donor is entitled to nothing beyond that. He may neither demand payment for its use nor claim compensation from the recipient, for the recipient bore liability for it and fed it in return for the benefit he derived from it.

original_text:
وَسُئِلَ - رَحِمَهُ اللَّهُ -:
عَنْ رَجُلٍ قَدَّمَ لِأَمِيرِ مَمْلُوكًا عَلَى سَبِيلِ التَّعْوِيضِ الْمَعْرُوفِ بَيْنَ النَّاسِ مِنْ غَيْرِ مُبَايَعَةٍ فَمَكَثَ الْغُلَامُ عِنْدَ الْأَمِيرِ مُدَّةَ سَنَةٍ يَخْدِمُهُ ثُمَّ مَاتَ الْأَمِيرُ:
 فَهَلْ لِصَاحِبِ الْمَمْلُوكِ التَّعَلُّقُ عَلَى وَرَثَةِ الْأَمِيرِ بِوَجْهِ: بِثَمَنِ أَوْ أُجْرَةِ خِدْمَةٍ أَوْ بِحَالِ مِنْ الْأَحْوَالِ؟
فَأَجَابَ:
نَعَمْ إذَا وَهَبَهُ بِشَرْطِ الثَّوَابِ لَفْظًا أَوْ عُرْفًا فَلَهُ أَنْ يَرْجِعَ فِي الْمَوْهُوبِ مَا لَمْ يَحْصُلْ لَهُ الثَّوَابُ الَّذِي اسْتَحَقَّهُ إذَا كَانَ الْمَوْهُوبُ بَاقِيًا؛ وَإِنْ كَانَ تَالِفًا فَلَهُ قِيمَتُهُ أَوْ الثَّوَابُ. وَالثَّوَابُ هُنَا هُوَ الْعِوَضُ الْمَشْرُوطُ عَلَى الْمَوْهُوبِ.
وَسُئِلَ:
عَنْ رَجُل أَهْدَى الْأَمِيرَ هَدِيَّةً لِطَلَبِ حَاجَةٍ؛
 أَوْ التَّقَرُّبِ أَوْ لِلِاشْتِغَالِ بِالْخِدْمَةِ عِنْدَهُ أَوْ مَا أَشْبَه ذَلِكَ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَخْذُ هَذِهِ الْهَدِيَّةِ عَلَى هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ أَمْ لَا؟
 وَإِنْ أَخَذَ الْهَدِيَّةَ انْبَعَثَتْ النَّفْسُ إلَى قَضَاءِ الشُّغْلِ وَإِنْ لَمْ يَأْخُذْ لَمْ تَنْبَعِثْ النَّفْسُ فِي قَضَاءِ الشُّغْلِ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَخْذُهَا وَقَضَاءُ شُغْلِهِ أَوْ لَا يَأْخُذُ وَلَا يَقْضِي؟
translated_text:
He—may Allah have mercy on him—was asked:

A man presented a slave to an emir in expectation of recompense, as is customary among people, without concluding a sale. The slave remained with the emir, serving him for a year, and then the emir died. Does the man who gave the slave have any claim against the emir’s heirs, whether for the slave’s price, payment for his service, or on any other grounds?

He replied:

Yes. If he gave him as a gift on condition of receiving recompense, whether expressly stipulated or understood by custom, he may take back the gift so long as he has not received the recompense to which he is entitled, provided the gifted property still exists. If it has perished, he is entitled to its value or the recompense. Here, “recompense” means the consideration stipulated in return for the gift.

He was asked:

A man gives an emir a gift to have a request fulfilled, to gain his favour, to obtain employment in his service, or for some similar purpose. Is it permissible to accept the gift under these circumstances?

If accepting the gift makes him inclined to attend to the matter, whereas without accepting it he feels no such inclination, is it permissible for him to accept it and attend to the giver’s business, or should he neither accept it nor attend to it?

original_text:
وَرَجُلٌ مَسْمُوعُ الْقَوْلِ عِنْدَ مَخْدُومِهِ إذَا أَعْطَوْهُ شَيْئًا لِلْأَكْلِ أَوْ هَدِيَّةً لِغَيْرِ قَضَاءِ حَاجَةٍ:
 فَهَلْ يَجُوزُ أَخْذُهَا؟
 وَإِنْ رَدَّهَا عَلَى الْمُهْدِي انْكَسَرَ خَاطِرُهُ:
 فَهَلْ يَحِلُّ أَخْذُ هَذَا أَمْ لَا؟
فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ، فِي سُنَنِ أَبِي دَاوُد وَغَيْرِهِ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ قَالَ 
{مَنْ شَفَعَ لِأَخِيهِ شَفَاعَةً فَأَهْدَى لَهُ هَدِيَّةً فَقَبِلَهَا فَقَدْ أَتَى بَابًا عَظِيمًا مِنْ أَبْوَابِ الرِّبَا}
 وَسُئِلَ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ عَنْ السُّحْتِ؟
 فَقَالَ:
 هُوَ أَنْ تَشْفَعَ لِأَخِيك شَفَاعَةً فَيَهْدِيَ لَك هَدِيَّةً فَتَقْبَلَهَا.
 فَقَالَ لَهُ:
 أَرَأَيْت إنْ كَانَتْ هَدِيَّةً فِي بَاطِلٍ؟ فَقَالَ ذَلِكَ كُفْرٌ 
{وَمَنْ لَمْ يَحْكُمْ بِمَا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ فَأُولَئِكَ هُمُ الْكَافِرُونَ}
 وَلِهَذَا قَالَ الْعُلَمَاءُ: إنَّ مَنْ أَهْدَى هَدِيَّةً لِوَلِيِّ أَمْرٍ لِيَفْعَلَ مَعَهُ مَا لَا يَجُوزُ كَانَ حَرَامًا عَلَى الْمَهْدِيِّ وَالْمُهْدَى إلَيْهِ. وَهَذِهِ مِنْ الرَّشْوَةِ الَّتِي قَالَ فِيهَا النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ 
{لَعَنَ اللَّهُ الرَّاشِي وَالْمُرْتَشِي}
 وَالرِّشْوَةُ تُسَمَّى 
" الْبِرْطِيلُ "
. 
" وَالْبِرْطِيلُ "
 فِي اللُّغَةِ: هُوَ الْحَجَرُ الْمُسْتَطِيلُ فَاهُ.
 فَأَمَّا إذَا أَهْدَى لَهُ هَدِيَّةً لِيَكُفَّ ظُلْمَهُ عَنْهُ أَوْ لِيُعْطِيَهُ حَقَّهُ الْوَاجِبَ:
 كَانَتْ هَذِهِ الْهَدِيَّةُ حَرَامًا عَلَى الْآخِذِ وَجَازَ لِلدَّافِعِ أَنْ يَدْفَعَهَا إلَيْهِ كَمَا 
{كَانَ النَّبِيُّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ يَقُولُ: إنِّي لَأُعْطِي أَحَدَهُمْ الْعَطِيَّةَ فَيَخْرُجُ بِهَا يَتَأَبَّطُهَا نَارًا قِيلَ يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ فَلِمَ تُعْطِيهِمْ قَالَ؟ يَأْبَوْنَ إلَّا أَنْ يَسْأَلُونِي وَيَأْبَى اللَّهُ لِي الْبُخْلَ}
 وَمِثْلُ ذَلِكَ إعْطَاءُ مَنْ أَعْتَقَ وَكَتَمَ عِتْقَهُ أَوْ أَسَرَّ خَبَرًا أَوْ كَانَ ظَالِمًا لِلنَّاسِ فَإِعْطَاءُ هَؤُلَاءِ: جَائِزٌ لِلْمُعْطِي حَرَامٌ عَلَيْهِمْ أَخْذُهُ.
 وَأَمَّا الْهَدِيَّةُ فِي الشَّفَاعَةِ:
translated_text:
And if a man whose word carries weight with his master is given food or a gift, not in return for having a request fulfilled, may he accept it? If returning it would hurt the giver’s feelings, is it lawful for him to accept it or not?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah. It is reported in Sunan Abī Dāwūd and elsewhere that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“Whoever intercedes for his brother, then accepts a gift that his brother gives him, has entered a great gateway to usury.”

Ibn Masʿūd was asked about unlawful gain. He replied, “It is when you intercede for your brother, and he gives you a gift which you accept.”

The questioner then asked him, “What if the gift is for something wrongful?” He replied, “That is disbelief:

‘And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed—then it is those who are the disbelievers.’”

For this reason, the scholars have said that if someone gives a person in authority a gift so that he will do something unlawful for him, it is forbidden for both the giver and the recipient. This is a form of bribery, concerning which the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“May Allah curse the bribe-giver and the bribe-taker.”

A bribe is also called “al-birtīl.” In its lexical sense, “al-birtīl” means a stone with an elongated mouth.

If, however, someone gives him a gift to make him cease his oppression of him, or to obtain a right that he is obliged to grant him, the gift is forbidden for the recipient, but the giver may give it to him. Thus, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to say:

“I give one of them a gift, and he goes away with it, tucking fire under his arm.” He was asked, “O Messenger of Allah, why do you give to them?” He replied, “They insist on asking me, and Allah does not allow me to be miserly.”

The same applies to giving something to someone who has freed a slave but concealed the manumission, or has kept some information secret, or oppresses people. Giving to such people is permissible for the giver, but accepting it is forbidden for them.

As for a gift given in return for intercession:

original_text:

translated_text:
such as when someone intercedes with a ruler on a man’s behalf to have an injustice against him removed, secure his rights, obtain an office he deserves, enlist him among the fighting troops—when he is entitled to this—or obtain for him a share of funds endowed for the poor, jurists, Quran reciters, devout worshippers or others—when he is an eligible beneficiary. In these and similar cases of intercession that help fulfil an obligation or put an end to something forbidden, accepting a gift is likewise impermissible. The giver, however, may offer what will enable him to secure his rights or ward off injustice. This is what has been transmitted from the early generations and the great imams.

Some later jurists permitted this, classifying it under “reward-based contracts.” This contradicts the Sunnah and the statements of the Companions and the imams, and is therefore mistaken. Such work serves the public interest, and undertaking it is either an individual or a collective obligation. If accepting a reward for such work were sanctioned, it would follow that appointments to office and distributions of revenues acquired without fighting, charitable funds and other resources would go to those who paid for them. Likewise, protection from injustice would be afforded to those who paid for it, while those who did not pay would receive neither appointments nor funds nor protection from injustice—even if they were more deserving and more beneficial to the Muslims than those who paid.

The benefit here is not a private benefit to the person making the payment that would justify taking a reward from him, as for recovering a runaway slave or a stray animal. Rather, the benefit is for the public at large—by which I mean the Muslims. Every position must be entrusted to the most suitable person available who is capable of fulfilling its duties. The stipends allotted to fighting men, prayer leaders, callers to prayer and scholars must be given to those most deserving and most beneficial to the Muslims. This is obligatory upon the ruler, and the Muslim community must assist him in it. Thus, taking a reward from a particular individual for this leads to these

translated_text:
matters being sought in return for payment. Seeking positions of authority is itself forbidden, so how much more so when payment is involved! It would follow that whoever was in a position to pay would be appointed and given funds, even if someone else were more deserving and better suited. Indeed, this would entail appointing the ignorant, the sinful and the wicked, while passing over the knowledgeable, just and capable; and granting military stipends to the sinful and to cowards incapable of fighting, while passing over upright, courageous men who benefit the Muslims. Such practices cause much corruption. If someone takes payment and intercedes for an undeserving person when another is more deserving, he may neither take the payment nor intercede; refraining from both is better. If, however, he takes payment and intercedes for the person most deserving and best suited, while passing over the undeserving, then withholding intercession while taking payment is more harmful than interceding for someone undeserving.

The intercessor whose request secures acceptance for his intercession should be told:

You must act with sincerity towards Allah, His Messenger, the leaders of the Muslims and the Muslims at large. This would be your duty even without such influence and wealth; how much more so when you possess them! You must give sincere counsel to the person with whom you intercede, explaining who deserves appointment, employment and financial support, and who does not. By doing so, you act sincerely towards the Muslims, and through obedience you act sincerely towards Allah and His Messenger, for this is among the greatest acts of obedience. You must benefit the deserving person by helping him obtain these things, just as you must pray, fast and strive in Allah’s cause.

As for a man whose word carries weight, if he partakes of food beyond the hospitality sanctioned by Islamic law, he must repay his host with something equivalent, or else refrain from partaking of the excess. Otherwise, his acceptance of this additional hospitality is like accepting a gift. He is then like a witness who gives testimony, or an intercessor who intercedes, in return for hospitality or payment. This is among the causes of corruption. And Allah knows best.

فَأَجَابَ:
الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ،
 إذَا كَانَتْ الْعَادَةُ الْجَارِيَةُ بِالتَّعْوِيضِ وَأَعْطَاهُ عَلَى هَذَا الشَّرْطِ فَإِنَّهُ يَسْتَحِقُّ أَحَدَ الْأَمْرَيْنِ:
 إمَّا التَّعْوِيضُ وَإِمَّا الرُّجُوعُ فِي الْمَوْهُوبِ. وَأَمَّا الْمَمْلُوكُ فَإِنَّهُ إذَا لَمْ يُعْتِقْهُ الْمَوْهُوبُ لَهُ فَإِنَّهُ يَكُونُ بَاقِيًا عَلَى مِلْكِهِ. وَأَمَّا أَوْلَادُهُ فَيَتَّبِعُونَ أُمَّهُمْ فَإِنْ كَانَتْ حُرَّةً فَهُمْ أَحْرَارٌ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مَمْلُوكَةً فَهُمْ مِلْكٌ لِمَالِكِهَا؛ لَا لِمَالِكِ الْأَبِ؛ إذْ الْأَوْلَادُ فِي الْمَذَاهِبِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ وَغَيْرِهَا يَتَّبِعُونَ أُمَّهُمْ فِي الْحُرِّيَّةِ وَالرِّقِّ وَيَتَّبِعُونَ أَبَاهُمْ فِي النَّسَبِ وَالْوَلَاءِ.
 وَإِذَا لَمْ يَرْجِعْ الْوَاهِبُ حَتَّى فَاتَ الرُّجُوعُ فَلَهُ أَنْ يُطَالِبَ الْمَوْهُوبَ لَهُ بِالتَّعْوِيضِ إنْ كَانَ حَيًّا وَفِي تَرِكَتِهِ إنْ كَانَ مَيِّتًا:
 كَسَائِرِ الدُّيُونِ. وَإِنْ كَانَ قَدْ عَتَقَ وَلَهُ أَوْلَادٌ مِنْ حُرَّةٍ فَهُمْ أَحْرَارٌ.
translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man presented a slave to a dignitary. The established custom was that anyone making such a presentation would receive the slave’s price or its equivalent, but he received nothing. The slave married, had children, and died. Are his children free or not? Are the original owner’s children entitled to inherit from the person concerned under the guarantee?

He replied:

Praise be to Allah.

If the established custom was to give compensation, and he gave the slave on that condition, he is entitled to one of two things: either compensation or the recovery of his gift. As for the slave, if the recipient has not emancipated him, he remains his property. His children follow their mother’s status: if she is free, they are free; if she is enslaved, they belong to her owner, not their father’s owner. According to the four schools of law and others, children follow their mother in freedom or slavery, and their father in lineage and the bond of patronage arising from emancipation.

If the donor did not reclaim the gift before its recovery became impossible, he may demand compensation from the recipient if he is alive, or claim it against his estate if he is dead, like any other debt. If the slave had been emancipated and had children by a free woman, they are free.

translated_text:
He—may Allah Most High have mercy on him—was asked:

A man bought a slave and gave him property until the slave became wealthy. It then emerged that the slave had actually been free. May he recover what he gave him in the belief that he was a slave?

He replied:

Yes, he may recover it.

He was also asked:

A man divorced his wife, asked her to reach a settlement, and settled with her. He recorded two dinars as due to her, then said to her, “Give me one of the dinars as a gift.” She did so, but he then divorced her. May she revoke the gift in these circumstances?

He replied:

Yes, she may revoke what she gave him in these circumstances, for he asked her for the gift and nevertheless divorced her. She had not wanted him to take her money at his request and then divorce her. And Allah knows best.
